speakeroldname: Right Hon. P. E. Trudeau (Prime Minister):
maintopic: BIRTHDAY CONGRATULATIONS TO HON. ROBERT L. STANFIELD
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, our presence here today is sufficient proof that good intentions are not always sufficient to produce the desired result. It had been the hope of those of us in this party that this House would not be making demands today on the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Stanfield), thus freeing him for leisurely activities more appropriate to this date. The fact that we are here, however, gives me the opportunity to extend to him our very best wishes and to tell him what we propose in order to mark this occasion.
The hon. gentleman knows that no statistics have emerged today which would be disturbing to him apart of course from his own accelerating annual adjustment over which the government has no control. We also continue to hold out the invitation to recess the sitting at an early hour. Finally, I wish to assure the hon. gentleman that we will understand completely should he decide to refrain from participating in the question period to enjoy a well deserved rest. But whatever his choice, the basic aspect of this message is not negotiable-we wish him a very happy birthday.

maintopic: BIRTHDAY CONGRATULATIONS TO HON. ROBERT L. STANFIELD
speechtext: Hear, hear!

maintopic: BIRTHDAY CONGRATULATIONS TO HON. ROBERT L. STANFIELD
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, there is nothing very much I can add to the humour the Prime Minister put into his best wishes, except to say that the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Stanfield) has now reached the age where I expect him to join with us in seeking a reduction in the age of eligibility for the old age pension. As you know, Mr. Speaker, the Leader of the Opposition and I have been engaged for a year and a half-

speechtext: Engaged?

maintopic: BIRTHDAY CONGRATULATIONS TO HON. ROBERT L. STANFIELD

speechtext: Hear, hear!

speechtext: -and that the Leader of the Opposition has been seeking a marriage for the same 18 months. On behalf of my colleagues, I want to wish him the very best on his birthday and whether or not he participates in the question period today or any other day, to wish him many years of active public life with the same sincerity and pleasantness he has shown so far.

maintopic: BIRTHDAY CONGRATULATIONS TO HON. ROBERT L. STANFIELD
speechtext: Hear, hear!

maintopic: BIRTHDAY CONGRATULATIONS TO HON. ROBERT L. STANFIELD
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I hope we are not here today for the sole purpose of celebrating the birthday of the hon. Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Stanfield). However, I believe it is customary and I am very pleased to do so on behalf of our party and wish him a very happy birthday. We hope that since we are here the day will be fruitful for the Canadian people.

speakeroldname: Hon. Robert L. Stanfield (Leader of the Opposition):
maintopic: BIRTHDAY CONGRATULATIONS TO HON. ROBERT L. STANFIELD
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am almost overcome. I wish to thank the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) and the leaders of the other parties who have expressed good wishes to me for the future. I am all the more touched when I realize how deeply sincere these wishes are, Mr. Speaker. I am, of course, pleased that everybody now recognizes why we are here today. The only thing I should like to make very clear is that, of course, the celebrations continue all next week.
Finally, may I say that I realize it would be very difficult for anybody, judging from my physical vigour, the rapidity of my speech in English and my eloquence in French, to believe that I have reached the sixth decade.

maintopic: BIRTHDAY CONGRATULATIONS TO HON. ROBERT L. STANFIELD
speechtext: The seventh decade.

maintopic: BIRTHDAY CONGRATULATIONS TO HON. ROBERT L. STANFIELD
speechtext: Whether it be the sixth or seventh, I am sure it does not compare at all with the tenth. The only real warning I should give the Prime Minister and his friends, the Leader of the New Democratic Party and my friends in the Social Credit Party of course is that on this anniversary, the achievement of this great age, and with the recognition that the time ahead of me is that much shorter, I have become more hungry for power than ever before.

maintopic: BIRTHDAY CONGRATULATIONS TO HON. ROBERT L. STANFIELD
speechtext: Hear, hear!

Mr. Speaker, I rise on a matter of urgent and pressing necessity under the provisions of Standing Order 43 arising from the very serious situation which prevails in the grain industry, as critically outlined by the chairman of the Canadian Wheat Board, Mr. Vogel at the National Transportation Conference yesterday. I therefore move, seconded by the hon. member for Calgary North:
That the federal government take immediate steps to ensure that the Canadian grain producers will be relieved of all costs and charges caused by contractual default by the Canadian Wheat Board for failure to meet sales commitments, and further, that all abnormal demurrage charges be paid for by the federal treasury since Canada's transportation system has failed to move sufficient quantities of grain to export position.

speakeroldname: Hon. Robert L. Stanfield (Leader of the Opposition):
subtopic: THE CANADIAN ECONOMY
subsubtopic: REQUEST FOR STATEMENT ON GOVERNMENT MEASURES TO CURB INFLATIONARY EXPECTATIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have a question for the right hon. the Prime Minister, and I am sure that on this day of all days I will get a very full and satisfactory answer. Yesterday, the Minister of Finance said that one of the basic causes of rapidly rising housing costs is that Canadians are buying houses to "protect themselves against inflation". In light of this apparently belated discovery by the Minister of Finance who has been previously attributing inflation to international phenomenon and shortage of supply, I should like to ask the Prime Minister whether the govern-
Oral Questions
ment has any specific measure in mind to break this inflationary psychology to which the minister referred yesterday?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. P. E. Trudeau (Prime Minister):
subtopic: THE CANADIAN ECONOMY
subsubtopic: REQUEST FOR STATEMENT ON GOVERNMENT MEASURES TO CURB INFLATIONARY EXPECTATIONS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I would refer the Leader of the Opposition to the statement of the minister. He indicated that this was one cause amongst many. It is reasonably well known that in inflationary times, and nobody denies that inflation is now higher than we would like to see it, people tend to go into commodities or into goods, away from money. The Minister of Finance added that they were choosing housing because of the exemption of capital gains on housing. That is a fair statement of the position of the Minister of Finance. In so far as specific measures are concerned, Mr. Speaker, yes, they are being contemplated by the government and will be announced in the appropriate manner.

subtopic: THE CANADIAN ECONOMY
subsubtopic: REQUEST FOR STATEMENT ON GOVERNMENT MEASURES TO CURB INFLATIONARY EXPECTATIONS
speechtext: A supplementary question, Mr. Speaker. Now, that we have this disclosure that inflationary expectations are an important factor in the increases in prices that are taking place, at least in some areas of the economy, has the Prime Minister prepared a new approach and has the government really got anything in mind to curb these inflationary expectations or is it just content to let things go on?

subtopic: THE CANADIAN ECONOMY
subsubtopic: REQUEST FOR STATEMENT ON GOVERNMENT MEASURES TO CURB INFLATIONARY EXPECTATIONS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, much of our action has been an attempt precisely to kill this inflationary psychology but we cannot hide from the Canadian people the fact that inflation is also largely caused by events beyond the control of the Canadian government and people. To this degree, we can only point out to them signs of an easing of international commodities prices which are becoming evident. Wholesale prices of grain, cattle, hogs, wool and cotton have already turned down, some very significantly. Metal prices will remain at a high level but the prices of such commodities as coffee and sugar have levelled out recently after a sharp rise. We hope that people will notice this, rather than responding to the panic which is encouraged in some quarters.

subtopic: THE CANADIAN ECONOMY
subsubtopic: REQUEST FOR STATEMENT ON GOVERNMENT MEASURES TO CURB INFLATIONARY EXPECTATIONS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the Prime Minister would not be old enough to remember, but I am just old enough to remember that this is the way a lot of people talked in the thirties about prosperity being just round the corner. Seriously, Mr. Speaker, I gather from what the Prime Minister said to me that it is simply the intention of the government to wait and hope that this situation will straighten out. Since the Prime Minister's explanation of inflation is that too many people are trying to take too much out of the economy, and since he said recently that organized labour is not responsible for this, can he tell the House who is taking too much out of the economy and what he proposes to do about it.

SUGGESTED EXTENSION OF TWO-PRICE SYSTEM TO COMMODITIES OTHER THAN OIL AND WHEAT-GOVERNMENT POSITION
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I am not going to ask questions about inflationary psychology and how to curb it, because I have never been able to understand what that phrase means and I suspect that those who use it do not understand it either.

subtopic: SUGGESTED EXTENSION OF TWO-PRICE SYSTEM TO COMMODITIES OTHER THAN OIL AND WHEAT-GOVERNMENT POSITION
speechtext: The Minister of Finance certainly does not understand what it means.

subtopic: SUGGESTED EXTENSION OF TWO-PRICE SYSTEM TO COMMODITIES OTHER THAN OIL AND WHEAT-GOVERNMENT POSITION
speechtext: It was the Leader of the Opposition who used it, Mr. Speaker. May I address my question to the Minister of Finance. As both he and the Prime Minister have rightly insisted that one of the causes of rising prices in Canada is the international shortage of some basic commodities and the international price increase of those commodities, including commodities produced in Canada in abundance for meeting the needs of Canadians, has the Minister of Finance given consideration to extending the principle and policy of the two-price system beyond oil and wheat, to cover other basic commodities produced in Canada, which should be made available to Canadians at a reasonable price rather than at the exorbitant international price?

speakeroldname: Hon. John N. Turner (Minister of Finance):
subtopic: SUGGESTED EXTENSION OF TWO-PRICE SYSTEM TO COMMODITIES OTHER THAN OIL AND WHEAT-GOVERNMENT POSITION
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I think one of the topics which should be before the House at the moment is the psychology of the hon. member for York South and his followers. While we have a two-price system on wheat and, to a certain extent, on petroleum, this two-price system, if carried to great lengths and supported by export controls and other types of mechanisms which would be needed to reinforce it, might well be considered as a new style of protectionism whereby this country would seek to protect its own price and supply structure at the expense of other nations, developing and developed. In terms of international trade, as this nation depends for one quarter of its gross national product on its relationships with other nations, I am not sure that it would be an unqualified advantage to accept the suggestion of the hon. gentleman.

subtopic: SUGGESTED EXTENSION OF TWO-PRICE SYSTEM TO COMMODITIES OTHER THAN OIL AND WHEAT-GOVERNMENT POSITION
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, setting aside what the Minister of Finance has to say about my psychology, I cannot understand his logic let alone his psychology. My suggestion has nothing to do with controlling in any way prices outside this country. I did not suggest that we should interfere with or control the normal export market, so that there would be no interference at all with what goes out of this country. I ask the Minister of Finance to tell this House and the people of Canada why Canadians should pay more for their commodities merely because other parts of the world are pushing up the price on what they produce.

subtopic: SUGGESTED EXTENSION OF TWO-PRICE SYSTEM TO COMMODITIES OTHER THAN OIL AND WHEAT-GOVERNMENT POSITION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, let me try
to get this on a logical basis. The hon. member and I will

then be on the same plane. If we are to have a two-price system on commodities whereby there is a lower domestic price than international price, then basic commodities would inevitably seek the higher international price unless we were to put export controls to ensure that that supply remains here. Export taxes or export control would be a new style of protection for our pricing and supply structure, which would be subject to retaliation by other nations, because it would be as potentially dangerous for Canada as an international trader as tariff barriers or invisible barriers were to protect our employment situation in the thirties.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: SUGGESTED EXTENSION OF TWO-PRICE SYSTEM TO COMMODITIES OTHER THAN OIL AND WHEAT-GOVERNMENT POSITION
speechtext:
The Chair will recognize the hon. member for York South for a supplementary.

-I shall then allow the hon. member for Abitibi to put a supplementary, after which I shall give the floor to several other hon. members who wish to put supplementaries.

subtopic: SUGGESTED EXTENSION OF TWO-PRICE SYSTEM TO COMMODITIES OTHER THAN OIL AND WHEAT-GOVERNMENT POSITION
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I will try to see if I can word this question so that Your Honour will not object to it as being debate. If there is any validity in what the minister said, will he explain to the House why he does not apply it to oil and wheat? Also, will he explain to the House and the people of Canada why protection for the Canadian consumer and the Canadian economy is something he rejects?

subtopic: SUGGESTED EXTENSION OF TWO-PRICE SYSTEM TO COMMODITIES OTHER THAN OIL AND WHEAT-GOVERNMENT POSITION
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I am interested in protecting the consumer and the Canadian economy, but in ways that will not jeopardize the long term trading interests of this country. The reason it was done for oil, of course, is that the price was not set domestically in Canada. It was set internationally by quasi-monopolistic practices in the Persian Gulf and by OPEC nations. Our two-price situation in oil was a defensive mechanism. The hon. member knows that full well.

At the present time, nearly all the papers published by the government say that the inflation is in part caused by the shortage of consumer goods. ACTION TO HELP WORKERS NOT PROTECTED BY UNIONS OR LARGE CORPORATIONS TO FIGHT INFLATION-GOVERNMENT POSITION
speechtext: A further supplementary to the minister arising from a very serious situation which has developed. It is based on the fact that average weekly wages have risen by 7.4 per cent while inflation is now running at 10.4 per cent, a difference of three percentage points. Can the minister tell us what immediate plans he has to protect the workers, who seem to get further and further behind?

speakeroldname: Hon. John N. Turner (Minister of Finance):
subtopic: ACTION TO HELP WORKERS NOT PROTECTED BY UNIONS OR LARGE CORPORATIONS TO FIGHT INFLATION-GOVERNMENT POSITION
speechtext: The action we took last year and this year in increasing the disposable income of wage earners has worked, and in terms of disposable income workmen in this country have improved their standard of living.

speechtext: I am sure that answer is not acceptable to those who are trying to buy food, clothing and housing. speechtext: I have a supplementary for the Prime Minister. speechtext:
The House resumed, from Wednesday, April 10, consideration of the motion of Mr. Turner (Ottawa-Carleton) that Bill C-14, to amend the Farm Improvement Loans Act, the Small Businesses Loans Act and the Fisheries Improvement Loans Act, be read the second time and referred to committee of the whole.
April 11, 1974

subtopic: FARM IMPROVEMENT, SMALL BUSINESSES AND FISHERIES IMPROVEMENT LOANS ACTS AMENDMENTS RESPECTING LOANS AND GOVERNMENT LIABILITY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, yesterday I had just started my remarks on this bill when we were interrupted for the purpose of going to the other place to attend some of their deliberations, and when we returned it was six o'clock. Therefore, I will continue my remarks now. As I recall, I had read a letter from one of my constituents in which he recounted the problems he had when he went to the bank to try to get a loan under the Small Businesses Loans Act. I believe I related the fact that I had sent a circular to all the small businesses in my riding acquainting them with the Small Businesses Loans Act and telling them that if they so desired they could get a loan from the banks at 8V4 per cent interest. Of course, when I did that I realized that no bank manager in my riding would be friendly toward me, but I thought that that information would be of assistance to small businesses in my community.
I found, on talking to businessmen, that chartered banks use various tactics to discourage them from borrowing money under the Small Businesses Loans Act. As I read from the letter I had received, one bank manager said he had never heard of the act. I found that some of the chartered banks use other tactics. For instance, in some areas they will assign one of the branches, perhaps in the most remote residential part of an urban area, to handle small business loans. The object, of course, is to make it as difficult as possible for the businessman, to put another obstacle in his way and to make him change the bank with which he deals.
We know that bank managers come back in a hurry and say, "We will lend you money at 11 VS per cent or 12 per cent." We also know that some bank managers may be frightened of the risk and will direct the customer to the Industrial Development Bank, where a person will pay 11'/2 per cent, 12 per cent or 13 per cent. It is usually higher than the going bank rate. We must look into these matters carefully.
In the 1972 bank report, in the column setting out loans under the various banks, we find that the Bank of Montreal-which advertises on television that it helps people- made 433 loans in the whole of Canada under the Small Businesses Loans Act. The Bank of Nova Scotia made 134 loans. It seems that the Royal Bank outdid everybody and made 952 loans. The Toronto-Dominion Bank found it in their heart to make 181 loans. The Mercantile Bank of Canada made one loan, so it must have made a mistake there. The Canadian National Bank made 741 loans. The Provincial Bank of Canada made 41 loans. The Canadian Imperial Bank of Commerce made 358 loans. The Bank of British Columbia made 4 loans. Credit unions made one loan. This is a total of 2,846 loans in all of Canada in 1972 under the Small Businesses Loans Act. I submit that in any city in Canada with a population of 200,000 or more any one bank could have made 2,846 loans.
It is all very well for the government to make loans available at a low interest rate, but the fact is that banks have not been interested in this program. I have asked the Minister of Finance (Mr. Turner) many questions in the House and in the committee regarding this matter and I have always received one of his usual cryptic replies, the type to which I think we can almost assign a number-it could be called reply No. 27: I will take the matter up with
Loans Acts Amendments
the chairman of the Canadian Bankers' Association when we have lunch next week.
That is the type of practice that we would like to see stopped. We would like to see the minister and bank managers get together. I appreciate that one of the problems the banks are facing is lack of liquidity: they are short of funds. I am sure that if they have money to lend, they want to lend it at the highest possible rate of interest; and as a businessman I cannot fault them for that because it is the normal course of commerce. But the liquidity situation has not always been as it is today. If we go back to 1971 and 1972 and look at the statistics produced in the report, we see that the highest number of loans ever made under the Small Businesses Loans Act is 2,977, and that was in 1961. Eleven years later, in 1972, the latest report that we have shows the banks only made 2,846 loans. This makes me question the sincerity of the minister and of the banks.
Something should be done for small businesses in this country. I am sure that all hon. members recognize weaknesses in small businesses. Some of them are specialists in everything but financing. I also recognize that they have many problems. But, as I said at the beginning of my remarks, small businesses are the backbone of and provide stability to Canadian commerce. They create over half of Canada's gross national product and employ over half of the working people in Canada. They rarely have lay-offs; they rarely have strikes. They pay their taxes and they pay their employees. They are the ones who keep the country going when other things go wrong.
When you look at the facilities that are available to small businessmen in the conduct of their businesses, you understand that if the government is really going to make a meaningful contribution toward helping small businesses it will have to amend the Bank Act in the near future. One of the problems of small businessmen is acquiring working capital. Small businesses are not labour-intensive and are usually not capital-intensive. But they are working capital-intensive. This is particularly important today in a situation of tight supply of materials. I have discussions with many small businessmen regarding the supply of steel, for instance. We find that the standard angles, channels and shapes are not available in the normal course of events, and in part this is because wholesalers are using the shortage of supply and tight money situation to their own advantage.
The small fabricator finds that if he places a c.o.d. order with a supplier, he gets the material right away; but if he places an order under the normal terms, in most cases the warehouse tells him to call back tomorrow and they just might have something for him. This all relates to the problem of working capital. The small businessman cannot exist unless he has money available, and if the prevailing situation requires him to pay cash for the supplies he needs in order to operate, he is soon in serious trouble.
I am glad the suggestion made yesterday to deal with this bill in committee of the whole, rather than sending it to the standing committee, was adopted. This will ensure getting the legislation into operation sooner than if it

April 11, 1974
Loans Acts Amendments
went to the finance committee, in view of the backlog of work of that committee. I hope the minister will read the remarks made by members of his own party regarding the difficulties encountered by fishermen, farmers and small businessmen when they apply for bank loans. It is all very well to increase the limit to $50,000, but with the present limit of $25,000 the average loan across Canada is only $9,500. I hope we will see a substantial increase in this respect and that many small businesses will be able to take advantage of the Small Businesses Loans Act provision for new businesses which is not available in the act as it now stands.
With those remarks I shall conclude, Mr. Speaker. I hope we can bring this debate to an end before whatever is going to happen, happens-I think you know what I mean-so that we will be able to pass on to the small business community whatever advantages will accrue to them from this amendment to the Small Businesses Loans Act.

subtopic: FARM IMPROVEMENT, SMALL BUSINESSES AND FISHERIES IMPROVEMENT LOANS ACTS AMENDMENTS RESPECTING LOANS AND GOVERNMENT LIABILITY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I just want to make a couple of very brief remarks with respect to this bill. Because it is divided in three, part of my remarks will relate to that section of it which deals with the Fisheries Improvement Loans Act. At the outset I should say that I wonder why the House is taking this tack and exerting its energy and consideration on something so insignificant and of so little value to fishermen as this bill. It just seeks to amend in a very slight way the amount of money that a fisherman may borrow from a bank or other lending institution for the purposes contained in the act. It seeks to extend from $25,000 to $50,000 the limit that a person can borrow. Anyone not familiar with the fishing industry could argue that this is a substantial alteration, but let me make a few comments with regard to the salmon fishery on the west coast for the sake of argument.
Five or six years ago the Minister of Fisheries instituted a licensing limitation program in the salmon industry. With the continual "early morning upon arising" changes that the minister announced respecting that initial program, to the point that very few fishermen knew what it was all about-because the change obviously was the result of a heavy meal before bedtime, which produced a rather nightmarish situation for the government-things have gradually cleared to the point that on the west coast there is a limitation on these licences: only a certain number are issued and no new ones are allowed. This has been the case in the taxi industry, in the forest industry and in every other industry where franchises are involved.
In the case of the fishing industry, the cost of the licence is more than the value of the boat to which it applies. The current selling price for a salmon licence on the west coast ranges from $3,500 and $4,000 per ton of fishing vessel. A very small troller of 36 feet to 38 feet which has a salmon licence can cost a fisherman from $65,000 to $75,000. He pays more for the licence than for the boat: the larger the boat, the greater its tonnage and therefore the higher the price. In that type of atmosphere a $50,000 limit under the provisions of this act is meaningless to the average fisherman. Therefore, it is hardly worth the House taking the time to listen to what the government has to say on the matter.

The other matter I want to mention is broader in application and relates to interest rates. All three of the acts being amended by this bill, the Farm Improvement Loans Act, the Small Businesses Loans Act and the Fisheries Improvement Loans Act, contain a provision relating to the rate of interest a financial institution or chartered bank may charge on a guaranteed loan. The rate may fluctuate. I do not know the current rate: one can ascertain this by 'phoning the bank. Probably the current rate is in the neighbourhood of 714 or 7Vi per cent.
Because interest rates are limited, the government guarantees the loan. No matter whether the default is by reason of insolvency or any other reason, the loan is guaranteed absolutely by the government of Canada. Therefore there is no possibility of the bank losing any of the capital involved. Originally, I suppose, the saw-off came in this way; the government said to the banks, "If you will agree to limit the rate of interest you will charge on these loans, we will guarantee the loans unconditionally."
I would argue that we should limit interest rates on moral grounds rather than on financial grounds. What are these moral grounds? The people with whom these acts deal are probably in the most vulnerable position in the business world. Being farmers and fishermen, they are primary producers who are subject to a great deal of economic pressure. They have little control over the price they receive for their produce and no control at all over the price they must pay for materials, commodities and services which are necessary if they are to maintain their farming, business or fishing operations. In short, they are at the mercy of large forces in society and are caught in this squeeze. Somebody else dictates what they will pay for their supplies and somebody else dictates, to a great degree, the price for which they can sell their produce, whether it is the produce of the farm, of the sea or of our fresh waters.
The small businessman is in the same position. He is not so much a producer as a provider of services which involve, for instance, retail distribution and things of that kind. He is at the mercy of the large pressure groups in our economy. My argument is this: because these people cannot exercise much leverage in the economy, it behooves us to pay greater attention to their economic position. Therefore we should limit the interest rates they must pay. Because interest rates are limited, banks, other lending institutions and credit unions-which, although more sympathetic perhaps than chartered banks, are still caught in the cost squeeze for money-are reluctant in some cases to lend. Lending institutions say to themselves, although not in public, "Why should we lend money under the Fisheries Improvement Loans Act at 7 !4 per cent when we can lend money to the fellow next door at 11 per cent?"- or whatever the going rate is.
If the prime bank rate is 9 Vi per cent, the most advantageous rate for a borrower would be 1 per cent higher. We are talking about a rate in the 10 Vi to 11 per cent bracket. The bank says to itself, "Why should we lend money under these acts at 7!4 per cent when we can lend it to somebody else at 10 Vi per cent? Why should we forgo 3 per cent interest?" Considering the fact that banks were estab-
April 11, 1974

lished in the first place to lend other people's money and not to provide any beneficial service except to themselves, one can understand that attitude. Why should they not operate on that basis? The person who suffers from that attitude is the individual fisherman, small businessman and farmer. The acts may guarantee loans and limit interest rates, but the farmer, businessman or fisherman finds it difficult to obtain money.
In a previous session, and again in this session, I brought forward a bill which would establish a different principle and concept with respect to lending under these acts. I submit that if it is public policy, and good public policy

which I submit it is-to limit the interest which lending institutions can charge, then we as the parliamentarians who have imposed that limitation must make sure that lending institutions do not discriminate against those entitled to borrow under these acts.
The bill I introduced contains a provision which ought to be incorporated in the bill before us. That provision is that lending institutions should be required to make available sums of money for lending under these acts which are not less than the average they have lent, say in the last five-year period. It really does not matter what period you use so long as you are consistent. That is to say, they should be required to make money available under these acts to potential borrowers, and they should not be allowed to refuse to lend money on the basis that they are not making a large enough profit on the loan. If an individual entitled to borrow under these acts goes to the bank, applies for a loan and on a logical and reasonable basis is refused a loan, that individual should have the right to appeal the decision of the bank to the Department of Finance or some structure within it. This body would assess the potential of the borrower and either say he was a poor risk and the bank was right, or he was a good risk and the bank was wrong, in which case it would direct the bank to make the loan.
It must always be kept in mind that these loans are underwritten and guaranteed by the people of Canada through the minister of finance and the government of Canada.
Unless we make some kind of effort in this direction we will find that the higher interest rates-and they will go higher-will work to the disadvantage of potential borrowers under these three acts. It will be more attractive for the banks and lending institutions to lend money at the higher going rate than under these acts.
At the moment, a number of banks are engaged in the practice of borrowing money from private individuals by means of term deposits. The banks borrow this money for a term of five or six years at an absolute guaranteed rate of 8'/2 per cent. There was an ad in yesterday's Ottawa Journal by some trust and loan companies. In letters six to eight inches high they guarantee an interest rate of 9 per cent for term deposits of up to five or six years. If lending institutions are going to commit themselves to carrying an 8 'A or 9 per cent liability on money that they borrow for five or six years, they are also going to commit themselves to charging higher interest rates on the money they lend.
Loans Acts Amendments
This will be necessary in order to obtain the money with which to pay the high interest rate.
The longer this situation is permitted to continue, the more we will be looking at a continuation of potentially higher interest rates. The more that happens, the more the general public will suffer with regard to interest rates on loans for housing and other things. However, because this bill is before us we have to relate our concern to it. The more that happens, the more our farmers, fishermen and small businessmen will be disadvantaged. They are now disadvantaged more than any other group in the entrepreneurial field which produces by its own efforts. In spite of the limitation increase from $25,000 to $50,000 for fishermen-regardless of how little value that is with today's costs, the value of fishing boats and the like-they will still be disadvantaged by the banking and lending institutions.
I have not considered the bill in any detail. I will do that at the committee stage. Because of the recommendation of His Excellency which confines the area to be considered in committee, I am not sure whether procedurally we can move amendments. I do not know whether the concepts I have included in a bill now before the House, and which I advanced a moment ago can be fitted into this bill. If it can be done at the committee stage, or possibly at the report stage, I hope to introduce these types of amendment so that the House and the committee will have an opportunity to express a view about the concepts I have advanced. That is supplementing the morality aspect and the recognition this parliament is giving to the needs of farmers, fishermen and small businessmen by the guarantee procedure and saying they will not be disadvantaged because some loan shark thinks it is more profitable to lend money other than under this act. If I can fit those amendments into the committee stage or the report stage, I will certainly do so.
I hope that with that brief introductory comment, members will give some thought to the ideas I have put forward. Hopefully, something of this nature will be written into the legislation to further protect the position of people who borrow under these acts.

speakeroldname: Mr. Charles E. Haliburton (South Western Nova):
subtopic: FARM IMPROVEMENT, SMALL BUSINESSES AND FISHERIES IMPROVEMENT LOANS ACTS AMENDMENTS RESPECTING LOANS AND GOVERNMENT LIABILITY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I intend to speak only briefly on this bill. However, often when one intends to speak briefly he gets carried away. Certain aspects of this bill are beneficial. On the whole, it is legislation we can endorse in principle and I hope it will be speedily passed by this House.
I would echo some of the remarks of the hon. member for Skeena (Mr. Howard) with regard to lack of real content in the bill in terms of what it will do for the fishermen of Canada. This legislation was first put into place in 1955 with a lower lending limit to fishermen. That limit was increased, and is to be increased again so that fishermen may obtain a maximum loan of $50,000. I suspect that with the degree of inflation we have experienced in this country, that increase in the ceiling is not as beneficial as the amount was when the legislation was originally conceived, in terms of total buying power.
As the hon. member suggested, the limitation does not take into consideration the changing nature of the fishing industry since 1955. In this day and age, fishermen operat-
1370

April 11, 1974
Loans Acts Amendments
ing a $50,000 boat are really confined to the inshore fishery. By "inshore" I mean within about 15 miles of the sea coast. On the coast of the part of Canada from which I come, fishermen find it necessary to range 200 to 300 miles in order to make a year's pay in dragging and long-lining operations.
The Department of the Environment enunciated a program for the fisheries that seems to be at cross-purposes, to some extent, with the measures proposed in this bill. The department is attempting to encourage fishermen on the east coast to think in terms of more far-reaching vessels in order to fish off the coasts of Labrador, Greenland, the Flemish cape and in southern waters where there are species of fish available which are not being harvested to the fullest extent. Such a vessel costs from $1 million to $1.5 million.
A fisherman interested in engaging in the fishery that is now the major push of the Department of the Environment would be excluded from participating in it if he were to rely for his financing upon commercial banks lending money under guarantees authorized by this act. If the resources of the fishermen are limited and there are very few who can put up the difference in capital between what they can borrow under this act and what such a vessel costs, then to that extent they are precluded from owning such a vessels in which to fishing.
It is encouraging to see that this government which has been prone to regulating and restricting production and unable to assist farmers, fishermen and small businessmen, that has been so intent upon regulating the fishery to the point where it is very difficult to make a living or to have the diversification necessary, because of restrictions on licences, and so on, is at least thinking in terms of making credit a little easier for the fishermen to obtain.
There may be a substantial gap in the intent of the statute and the result it will produce. One of the members of the party to which I belong spoke yesterday of the success, if you like, of this plan as a means of financing fishermen in the Atlantic region. I would point out that each of the Atlantic provinces has its own loan board which advances money to fishermen at various rates of interest. In Newfoundland the rate of interest is very low. In Nova Scotia it is high in relation to the income a fisherman borrowing money under this proposal could earn.
In Nova Scotia there has been a dramatic increase in the amount of money lent to fishermen under this scheme in the past year compared to the previous year, but even in that province more than twice the amount of money was lent by the Nova Scotia fishermen's loan board to fishermen as was lent by commercial banks under this program. It has been suggested by speakers before me, and I think it is an easy conclusion to draw, that there are good reasons for this situation. One is that the banks are more willing to lend at a much higher rate of interest to other borrowers, or to fishermen borrowing on a straight loan. And, of course, as far as loans by the Nova Scotia fishermen's loan board are concerned, the arrangements are a little more realistic. The repayment term under this legislation is ten years, but a slightly longer term is provided under the

Nova Scotia fishermen's loans act. The time during which the debt can be repaid corresponds more or less with the productive life of the fishing vessel.
Under this legislation, though, only fishermen acquiring small boats, or prepared to carry out no more than minimal repairs, are able to borrow funds adequate enough for their purposes. Under the Nova Scotia fishermen's loan act a fisherman is able to borrow whatever money he needs, less 25 per cent. Thus, in the case of a vessel costing $1 million, if a fisherman is able to scrape up $200,000 or $250,000 he can purchase a ship capable of ranging in the offshore areas.
Under this scheme, if he arranged for a loan from the bank repayable in ten years, he would still be looking for a further $950,000. It follows that anyone who is interested in this kind of fishing would find such arrangements prohibitive. To give hon. members some idea of the costs involved in my area, let me say that the cost of a motor alone, of the kind commonly installed on an inshore fish dragger, is about $40,000. This alone would exhaust the amount one might borrow from a bank, even taking the present amendments into account. The provision of salt water cooling facilities in the hull of a vessel would account for $75,000 or more. A boat capable of fishing in a number of fisheries, sufficiently diversified to enable it to operate as a midwater trawler engaging in the herring and groundfish fisheries, would cost between $300,000 and $500,000.
Thinking in these terms, the act is obviously way behind the times. It will not help in any meaningful way fishermen such as I have just mentioned. I suggest it runs at cross-purposes with an objective which the Department of Fisheries' is seeking to achieve, since the act will not help our fishermen to compete with foreign vessels which are fishing in inshore areas and stripping our fisheries of their marine resources.
A striking divergence exists between amounts loaned under the act in various areas. Nova Scotia and British Columbia have fishing fleets which I assume are of approximately the same size. The value of fish landed is approximately the same in Nova Scotia as in British Columbia. Yet British Columbia fishermen had borrowed under this act, up to December, 1973, more than $2 million, while Nova Scotia fishermen had borrowed only $420,000- approximately 15 per cent of the amount of money loaned. Almost 80 per cent has been going to the coast of British Columbia.

I would suggest that the alternatives provided for the benefit of fishermen are not as numerous as they might be. It is encouraging that the government should be considering ways of enabling fishermen to finance the upgrading of their equipment and to purchase new equipment. It is, however, discouraging that the minister should have acted in such a penny-pinching way. The object should be to put into fisheries as much money under the provisions of this act as is currently being put into small businesses of other descriptions.
The concept put forward by the hon. member for Skeena would require the banks to lend money to the fishermen. That is an interesting concept. It would have an obvious difficulty in that it would require additional regulation, and it is apparent to everyone that the banks are reluctant to lend money under guaranteed lending schemes with fixed interest rates. Bank managers and the banking institution as a whole are reluctant to make such loans because they know low interest rates limit the amount of profit they can generate.
I suggest to the minister that in considering revisions to this act it would be worth while to consider making money available under its provisions for the purchase or upgrading of equipment used by fish dealers and small fish plant operators. I suppose they can qualify under this legislation, but such provision would seem to fall more readily, for administrative purposes, under the provisions of the Small Businesses Loans Act.
This bill does contain encouraging aspects and I hope it will be dealt with by the House in the manner suggested by other members of this party.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to say a few words on Bill C-14 which is divided into three parts and is designed to promote small businesses.
Mr. Speaker, I must say that small businesses like many other business enterprises, are in a most desperate situation. They provide many jobs for Canadians. I think that a high percentage of the labour force is employed by small industries which contribute a great deal to the transportation sector, because they are usually located rather far from large centres and have very high transportation costs.
Federal and provincial governments make fantastic amounts of money in transportation.
In my opinion, small businesses are needed and should exist. Moreover, I am one of those in favour of helping small businesses because they operate in all areas. You
Loans Acts Amendments
should see all the goods manufactured by small enterprises. At present, most small businesses are facing financial problems due to an imbalance in the economy.
As the cost of living increases and the cost of transportation and labour doubles or triples, small industries, like all other industries, have to raise their prices because they have to buy machinery and equipment. They must also double or triple their prices. Therefore, small businesses lack capital. Banks or financial institutions used to advance $25,000 to small industries under the legislation adopted by the government. Those $25,000 are not worth anything now because of the increase in the cost of living. About ten years ago, industries could buy machinery for $5,000 or $6,000, but today the same machinery costs $25,000. What can they do with a $25,000 loan? Because this small loan is granted to some industry by a bank, guaranteed by the government and by a first mortgage, the industry is cornered and can no longer operate, because $25,000 are not enough. Since it is a first mortgage, the industry can not borrow more and is caught by this very system. In the past, the $25,000 loans system for small business was better than nothing. It was convenient then for small businesses, but today it is ridiculous, it is clearly inadequate because if a man wants to buy one single piece of equipment for $15,000, $20,000 or $25,000, he will have to settle for second best. One single piece of equipment can cost that much and we know that an industry needs more than one.
The bill proposes to increase the loans to $50,000. Once again it is better than nothing, but it is inadequate for small businesses would need loans of at least $100,000 because everything is so expensive. What can anyone build with $50,000 when employees are paid $8 or $9 an hour and materials sell for prohibitive prices? Thousands of dollars do not last long. With four or five employees, any building can cost $25,000 to $30,000. What can you do with that? Mr. Speaker, some small businesses will be crippled with loans of only $25,000.
All hon. members and all Canadians know that small businesses are not allowed capital stock. Businesses with capital stock can operate because there is no need in this case to repay interests. We do not have to pay back but 75 per cent of small industries in the province of Quebec are unable to issue any capital atock. So they have to borrow, pay interests, and pay back. This paralyses them.
Mr. Speaker, this type of loan should be increased to at least $100,000 and should be payable over a period of 20 years at an interest rate lower than 3 per cent since the government backs them up and it is for the good of the people of this country.
Mr. Speaker, all sorts of measures are introduced, such as the Opportunities for Youth Program and the Local Initiatives Program, millions and millions of dollars are spent to subsidize useless things, and 75 per cent of those amounts are being wasted. Some industries could use them and hire young unemployed students who want to earn money. But no, they are given loans and grants of $1,000, $50,000 and even $100,000, Mr. Speaker, which in 80 per cent of cases are simply being wasted and do not benefit the economy.
This does not create any asset for the economy whereas if those monies were given to small and medium industry
1372

April 11, 1974
Loans Acts Amendments
to hire those people, show them how to work, make men out of them, small industry would benefit from it and working people or students would be learning something. We would be building something for this country, we could have cheaper products and consequently bring prices down.
If interest rates in small industry were only 3 per cent we would not have today an unprecedented increase in the cost of living, daily increases in all sectors. What I ask for small industry I also ask for farming and all sectors of society because if funds were made available at low interest rates they would produce a lot, and more cheaply. Society would then feel much better and we would enjoy price reductions as well as a lower cost of living instead of incurring price increases.
In connection with inflation, Mr. Speaker, it is easier to have a full purse than pay more at each purchase.
Price increases hurt, but a well-lined purse is nice. We should keep alert and one day set up a system which would enable the citizens to be self-sufficient in a wealthy country.
We are told it cannot be done because there is a shortage of commodities. If there is a shortage of commodities at the present time in various sectors of the economy, strikes and unions are crippling production. This is why there is a lack of goods and the cost of living is increasing. At the present time, unions are going too far and it is the duty of the government to cope with those conditions.
There are no longer any limits, Mr. Speaker. It is quite well to increase wages, to increase this and that. It is quite well to say the boss is making money, but 75 per cent of the bosses earn less, while working 10 to 15 hours a day, than some of their employees. The bosses earn less despite all their responsibilities.
Mr. Speaker, those small industries are providing the federal, provincial, municipal and school funds. Small firms are overtaxed to the extreme by school boards and municipalities alike.
A large number of municipalities entice small firms with promises. No sooner are they established that they are choked by taxes. A few years later, they are forced into bankruptcy.
Moreover, Mr. Speaker, small firms are being exploited-nobody mentions this, so I will tell you myself-by insurance companies. They are forced to mortgage their assets to buy insurance. These insurances choke industrialists and small businessmen alike. The premiums are much too high, Mr. Speaker. Nobody cares to say anything about this. We behave as though this was a trifle, like financing or 10 to 12 per cent interest rates. This seems somewhat sacred. When there is an increase in interest rates, nobody bats an eye. This seems somewhat sacred too. Mr. Speaker, there should be a limit to the exploitation of society.
We know that our ten Canadian financial institutions made more than $15 billion. This year, the increased their assets to more than $15 billion apart from another $15 billion which was concealed in some reserves. So we can say that our financial institutions increased their assets

by some $30 billion. No one says a word about that. The NDP particularly does not say anything. They wish to cut the throat of producing corporations that make profits but they have nothing against the financial institutions which are fleecing Canadians and make excessive profits.
So, Mr. Speaker, in order to balance our economy we need certain fair standards because there must be some justice. Everywhere, in every part of society we are exploited to death to such a point, that I could foretell, even if I am not a prophet, that if our present system continues to operate as it does now, terrible disasters are bound to occur within ten years. It will surely break somewhere if we do not act to stop inflation, reduce interest rates and the cost of living to allow Canadian to have a decent living. If we do not act, the present system will not survive a long time. The debts and the deficits we are now accumulating cannot past for ever. Out of 20 years of administration, all governments, whether they were red or blue, did finish two fiscal years with two small surpasses and 18 years with deficits. This year, and the Minister of Finance (Mr. Turner) knows it very well, we will have another deficit as usual. And in order to balance the government's budget we have to debalance the budget of taxpayers and then, in order to balance a little the budget of taxpayers we debalance that of the government. This means that our economy is badly organized and directed. This means also that in all sectors of society, we ought to apply remedies, and we have been suggesting some for a long time. And as long as the Minister of Finance does not find anything other than what we have now, things will keep on getting worse. Our economy keeps on tumbling down. Indeed, there is no balance in it.
Mr. Speaker, Canada is like a big company. We are all shareholders in that firm and we have to participate in it through taxes. But we are pressurized by taxes and our company is always in the red. Are there any private firms or financial institutions which would work this way? I do not think so. If we have a company into which we keep on investing money and which never shows any profit and if we keep on showing a deficit, our society is sick and needs some remedies. Mr. Speaker, we have suggested several adjustments: lower interest rates, compensated discounts on prices, on transportation, discounts for farmers, compensated discounts on tractors, on railways. To pay for this, Mr. Speaker, to give these compensated discounts on prices, we would have to collect the money from the profits of large comtjanies and large financial institutions.
When we have an overproduction of $25 or $30 billion, we are certainly able to provide compensated discounts to distribute this overproduction which belongs to everybody. Since Canada belongs to the people to each Canadian should receive his share of the assets that nature and the work of man have produced.
The small business sector needs many reforms. Even with a $50,000 loan to the small industry, we will not be able to save it. It would provide a certain stimulus, it would help the small business, extend its years of operation, but it would not solve the problem. The small business would still be in stagnation just like agriculture is in stagnation.
A few years ago, the hon. Mr. Duplessis had saved agriculture thanks to farm loans and the federal govern-
April 11, 1974

ment had also saved agriculture thanks to its farm loans, assistance plans and subsidies of all kinds.
More than ever today, agriculture is in stagnation. Industry faces the same problem. Since big business can automatically finance its operations by issuing shares or social capital, small business has much difficulty in competing against these large corporations. They need the help of politicians because otherwise, they will close down, which will increase the number of unemployed in our country by hundreds of thousands.
If we want the people to work instead of just receiving unemployment insurance or social assistance benefits, if we really want to have them work logically, loyally, to have them build what has to be built throughout the country, to demolish what no longer works, we will modernize Canada.
We need loans at very low interest rates. This government can grant those loans, if it so wishes. Instead of accepting higher interest rates as we can foresee now, it can make them go down. Why does it not guarantee a 3 per cent interest rate for our industries and other sectors of our economy? We would then have a new boom and the economy would be better balanced. There would be more motivated people willing to build more than to demolish, as is the case today.

subtopic: FARM IMPROVEMENT, SMALL BUSINESSES AND FISHERIES IMPROVEMENT LOANS ACT AMENDMENTS RESPECTING LOANS AND GOVERNMENT LIABILITY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to take part in this debate on the amendments to the Farm Improvement Loans Act. This act has been of great benefit to the farmers over the years as a source of readily available money. It has been accessible to the farmers through the banking and other lending institutions in every area.
Everyone would agree with the amendment raising the amount of a loan from $25,000 to $50,000: it is just keeping up with inflation and farm input costs. The price of tractors has gone up from $10,000 to as high as $25,000. The same is true of combines. It does not take very long to eat up the present maximum of $25,000. Also, the amendment to the act will allow farmers to borrow for the overhaul of tractors and farm machinery. It will be welcomed by many as the cost of overhauling large tractors is sometimes in excess of $2,000.
Other amendments allow the removal of limits and permit a person to borrow the whole amount on land and use it in the way he sees fit. This might create a problem because if each farmer can borrow up to $50,000 on the purchase of land, a tremendous amount of money will be funnelled into the purchase of land and there will be a heavy drain on the money supply. Since the inception of the act nearly 30 years ago, $3 billion have been lent and in the next 12 months, if the money is made available, $1 billion could be lent. In fact, the $1.1 billion which the government will guarantee to banks could easily be used up before June, 1977, the date mentioned in the bill.
I see a conflict between borrowing under the Farm Improvement Loans Act and under the Farm Credit Corporation Act, and I am pleased that the government has seen fit to bring in this legislation before its other very high priority, football legislation. I would rather have seen amendments to the Farm Credit Corporation Act brought in first and then the Farm Improvement Loans Act amendments to add to the farmer's credit requirements. I think there will be a heavy drain on this fund for land because at present under the Farm Credit Corporation Act

April 11, 1974
Loans Acts Amendments
money can be lent only on the appraised value of land, which amounts to about 60 per cent or 65 per cent of its actual market value, and under the Farm Improvement Loans Act money can be lent on 75 per cent of the market value.
Therefore, all these people who are refused loans under the Farm Credit Corporation Act will be heading back to the banks and other lending institutions and demanding loans under the Farm Improvement Loans Act for the purchase of land. This may have the effect of increasing the cost of land, which is rising rapidly as it is, and the result could be disastrous.
One of the shortcomings of the legislation is that one does not know where the money will come from. I cannot see banks or lending institutions advancing money for the purchase of land at 814 per cent or, for the other purposes outlined in the act, at 8 per cent. I have spoken to quite a few banks and credit unions in my area. They are not having any trouble lending money for equipment and quite a variety of things to farmers at 1014 per cent or 954 per cent, which is the prime rate. The government is guaranteeing loans by banks at 814 per cent, and banks are lending all the money they can at 914 per cent and 1014 per cent. Banks and credit unions in Saskatchewan are offering depositors a return of 814 per cent on their deposits and the government agrees to back loans at 8 per cent. It does not seem possible that banks will make money available at these low interest rates.
In discussions with various chartered bank managers in my area I have found that some of them have been discouraging FILA loans and some have been reserving the money for certain of their customers. Some banks are not even willing to lend money under the FILA. It is easy to see why, since they can make a loan on equipment at a much higher interest rate. Farmers have the equipment in their possession and the banks are not worried about security. So guaranteeing loans at 814 per cent is not advantageous to the banks.
The hon. member for Saskatoon-Biggar (Mr. Gleave) suggested that this bill would be doing a great favour to the banks, but quite a few of the bank managers to whom I spoke did not see it that way at all. In fact, they thought quite the reverse. One of them suggested that they would probably require $100 million in the next 12 months to make loans which people would request in that short time. The bill suggests that loans be made for cattle purchases. Of course, in Saskatchewan under certain conditions farmers are able to borrow for the purchase of cattle at a 7 per cent interest rate. I do not expect many farmers will borrow money under FILA at 8 per cent if they can get it at 7 per cent.
I agree with the amendment, Mr. Speaker. I can see that it removes some of the problems, but I am afraid the money will not be made available unless at a higher interest rate, which is probably coming anyway.
One reason for the heavy drain on money is the cost of machinery and labour and the shortage of people on the prairies trained in the repair of machinery. If more labour had been available in my area in the past there would not have been such heavy expenditures of capital. In France,

for example, there are about three million migrant workers, and in Switzerland one million. If the government is anxious to help farmers and small businessmen they can do it by helping overcome the labour shortage on the farms and small businesses in the west.

subtopic: FARM IMPROVEMENT, SMALL BUSINESSES AND FISHERIES IMPROVEMENT LOANS ACT AMENDMENTS RESPECTING LOANS AND GOVERNMENT LIABILITY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I want to add just a few remarks to the debate on Bill C-14 which amends the Small Businesses Loans Act, the Fisheries Improvement Loans Act and the Farm Improvement Loans Act primarily to allow for increasing the maximum amount of loans to $50,000 from the present $25,000. Nobody can quarrel with the amendment, but I have been very concerned about government guaranteed loans as they apply in my province. The increase in the maximum amount of the loans to half a million dollars is all very well, but my province is not receiving any benefit from this. I should like to quote from the latest reports. For example, under the Fisheries Improvement Loans Act in the period October 1, 1973, to December 31, 1973, Newfoundland received 14 loans amounting to $35,000. So what difference does it make whether the maximum amount is $25,000 or $50,000? Even Prince Edward Island received 40 loans amounting to $89,000. Something is wrong, Mr. Speaker, and I know what it is.
According to the latest report of the Small Businesses Loans Act for the period October, 1973, to December, 1973, Newfoundland received two loans amounting to $50,000; from January, 1973, to December, 1973, there were six loans. There must have been a good bank manager at that time. Under the Farm Improvement Loans Act, for the same period, Newfoundland did not receive any loans, and from January to December, 1973, there were three loans amounting to $8,788. In 1972, Newfoundland received four loans under the program, amounting to $6,500. The reason is that the agency responsible for carrying out the programs, the chartered banks, did not trust the small man to whom these programs are directed. I have evidence to show that they steer fishermen, farmers and small businessmen away from government loans because of the preferred rate of interest and, instead, guide them toward conventional loans which carry a high rate of interest.
Just recently I gave the Minister of Finance (Mr. Turner) an example where a fisherman, having taken his loan over three years, started out paying 8 per cent interest. In the half-year adjustment the rate of interest dropped to 6 'A per cent, but he was charged 8 per cent for the duration of the loan. I can name 18 or 20 loan programs designed either by the federal government or the provincial governments, or under the auspices of both on a co-ordinated basis, directed toward the farmer, the fisherman, the sawmill operator, storekeeper or small businessman-and all they do is cause confusion.
Just a few days ago we gave first reading to a bill introduced by the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Gillespie) to establish a new federal bank. It apparently is going to take over from the Industrial Development Bank. Industrial Development Bank loans are a last resort. If you cannot get anything from the mean bank manager, you go to the Industrial Development Bank. But before you can get a loan there-and you spend two or three years in the effort-they want to take your wife and
April 11, 1974

family and everything else as security. So you give up in frustration.
Under the federal and provincial governments a new corporation was recently formed in Newfoundland, called the Newfoundland and Labrador Development Corporation. It was also designed to grant loans to small businessmen. It has a big staff, a board of directors and offers consultative services and management advice, the same as the Industrial Development Bank and, I am sure, the new bank proposed by the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce. All that happens is that the borrower becomes more frustrated, and in the end he gets a letter saying that he does not qualify for a loan. These programs are there just because it is politically advantageous at some time or other to announce them.
An agricultural capital assistance program was announced recently in Newfoundland, where a prospective farmer can borrow up to $6,000 plus $200 per acre of eligible farm land and money for other purposes. This is another program just to confuse the issue. Under agreement with the federal government and the province of Newfoundland, there is the rural development loans program under which a small businessman may borrow $10,000 interest-free. Under the general development agreements there are many other programs and development incentives, all substantially directed to the small businessman, the farmer and the fisherman; but still most applicants are told that they do not qualify for any loan. I wish the government would consolidate all these programs that are directed toward the one borrower, instead of designing so many different ones. Banks should be made to realize that they have a duty to Canadians.
This is all I have to say on the bill, Mr. Speaker, because many of my colleagues have dwelt on other areas. I counted 18 programs, all with the same purpose but all working against each other to the detriment of the persons they are supposed to help. The government should examine their programs very carefully.

subtopic: FARM IMPROVEMENT, SMALL BUSINESSES AND FISHERIES IMPROVEMENT LOANS ACT AMENDMENTS RESPECTING LOANS AND GOVERNMENT LIABILITY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as I learned we are not going home I thought I might as well make a speech. My remarks will be as brief as I can make them. Being the ninth or tenth speaker in this debate it is safe for me to assume that if pertinent points have not been made, they have at least been implied. It is important for those representing smaller communities in which there are farmers, fishermen and businessmen, to take an interest in this bill. There are sizeable numbers of such people in my constituency and therefore I am interested in the sort of federal assistance which is suggested by this bill.
I was in the House when we debated in the fall of 1968 the Farm Improvement Loans Act, the Fisheries Improvement Loans Act and also, I believe, the Small Businesses Loans Act-that troika of bills designed to assist people who do not have resources for self-help and need to rely on government programs. I was interested in the remarks of the hon. member for Humber-St. George's-St. Barbe (Mr. Marshall). I feel that he illustrated very well the basic difficulty with this troika of assistance to small businessmen, farmers and fishermen. He suggested that, sure the legislation is before us, but few people ever get
Loans Acts Amendments
the loans. I think most of us have had the experience of constituents writing and asking about the kinds of services, the kinds of programs which are available to meet their particular needs. You write back and send them a whole portfolio of pamphlets dealing with ARDA, AIDA, PAIT, the IDB, and so on. You search through this great plethora of programs and when you want to find out if they are eligible, too often you find that they are not. You search through this great maze of programs in order to find out if there is one under which they qualify.
In my office we have a volume of pamphlets describing these programs, which we call the "money book". If somebody writes and asks about grants of one kind or another, we thumb through the "money book", fish out the relevant material, the advertising pamphlet promoting the program which best suits the constituent's needs, and send it out. I do not recall one of my constituents ever getting one of these grants, but at least we send out the literature. That is not good enough. If these programs are not to be mere tokenism, a mere pretense for helping the small businessman, farmer or fisherman, they ought to be consolidated as previous speakers have suggested. Further, the government should, like CMHC, make direct loans. This program should be handled as loans are now being handled by provincial corporations and the Farm Credit Corporation, rather than by way of guaranteed bank loans. Direct lending might help many people who need the service, because those who make use of these government programs are people without the kinds of resources which are needed for guarantees: the government acts as their guarantor.
In theory, this program works out nicely except when an individual goes to the bank and tries to take out a loan under the Farm Improvement Loans Act, the Fisheries Improvement Loans Act or the Small Businesses Loans Act; then he is usually deflected away from such a loan by the bank manager. I can understand this. The bank manager explains that the banks have only so much money to lend, and so on. Naturally, the bank prefers to lend at the higher interest rate of 12 per cent for a personal loan than at the guaranteed 8 per cent rate under this legislation. So the bank manager steers the prospective borrower to one of these higher-priced loans and away from the guaranteed loan as described in Bill C-14 because the bank is in the business of making profits.
My party has suggested that some of the funds of financial institutions should be devoted to mortgages at 6 per cent. That proposal was not embraced enthusiastically or affectionately-I think the latter word is preferable-by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Turner). He is not embracing anybody affectionately at the moment but seems to be consulting himself in dark seclusion.
