speechtext: He is on the side of the profiteers.

subtopic: FARM IMPROVEMENT, SMALL BUSINESSES AND FISHERIES IMPROVEMENT LOANS ACT AMENDMENTS RESPECTING LOANS AND GOVERNMENT LIABILITY
speechtext:
As the hon. member for Skeena (Mr. Howard) suggests, he is not on the side of the angels but on the side of the profiteers. Let us not kid the public about this program. It does not really matter if you raise the guaranteed ceiling to $50,000 for the period 1974 to 1977, if the banks will not lend money. And we are not speaking only of the banks. Something very interesting came to my attention when the fisheries committee was holding hear-

April 11, 1974
Loans Acts Amendments
ings in Vancouver in 1969. I will not name the particular institution. Representatives of a credit union run by fishermen came before us. Do you know what their chief complaint was? This is a credit union which accepts deposits from fishermen, is run for the advantage of fishermen and makes loans to fishermen, presumably in the interest of fishermen. Their chief complaint was that the level of interest they could charge under the Fisheries Improvement Loans Act was too small to permit them to pay the kinds of dividends their depositors wanted. This happened with an institution which lends to fishermen. I do not know the situation with regard to the Alberta Treasury or the near-banks, or whatever they are called, in that province; I am sure, nonetheless, that the same thing happens with other financial institutions authorized to make loans under these acts.
We say that if we are to provide this money, why not provide it through a Crown corporation such as CMHC, or lend it directly as is the case with the Farm Credit Corporation? At least there should be a provision in this bill demanding that financial institutions make available some portion of their funds to people who apply for loans under these acts. If we do not do that, what will we have? We will have filled this chamber with hot air for another afternoon and passed another bill-but nobody will really benefit. What is the use of the bill if the banks decide they do not want to lend money under the act?
The hon. member for Humber-St. George's-St. Barbe gave us an explicit breakdown of the scale of lending in Newfoundland under the Fisheries Improvement Loans Act over past years. If what he said was not a devastating attack on the futility of the nonsense, I do not know what is. Here we are, ready to deal with this bill in committee of the whole this afternoon. We think that if we pass it we will really have done something. But we will really not have done anything. That is what upsets me, because it seems that we are debating irrelevancies. Merely because we have provided guarantees does not mean that the banks will lend.
What happens if a borrower is not eligible for a loan from the banks under ARDA, AIDA, PAIT or any other provincial or federal corporation? We say, "Why do you not visit the friendly bank of last resort, the International Development Bank?" Instead of lending the borrower money at 8 per cent, in all probability it will charge between 10l/2 and 12 per cent because the risk is greater. Why can we not limit the risk with regard to loans made by the IDB in the same way as we limit risks with regard to ordinary loans made under this program? If we can guarantee loans made under this program by private banks, why cannot we enlarge the idea and extend the same sort of guarantee to the Industrial Development Bank?
Perhaps my last remark reveals my naivete and lack of familiarity with the workings of the IDB, but the question is pertinent. The banks, of course, prefer to lend at higher interest rates. Even if the interest rate were increased, the banks would prefer to steer borrowers to higher-rate-of-interest personal loans or to revolving credit accounts at 18 per cent. I think it is essential for us to come to grips with this question. If there is a trend in this country and in the country to the south of us, it is the trend of bigness.

We see it in many aspects. We see it when we fly in 747s. We see it when large supermarket chains come into a town and put the small grocery stores out of business.
Someone once said, and I cannot confirm whose words they are, that if you nationalized all businesses in this country having over 500 employees, after the nationalization or takeover most people would still be working for small businesses. Therefore, small businesses are a much larger employer in this country than large businesses. If we cannot stimulate small business in this country, we are destroying an opportunity to stimulate employment. I assume that is an objective of the government, although I sometimes wonder about it with unemployment running around 600,000 people, or 6 per cent, for the past year. Whether another government could do anything about that, I do not know. However, it seems that if it were possible to stimulate more small businesses, and if the logic that small businesses are the greatest employers of people in Canada is correct, we would be doing something to assist the unemployment problem.
I am not particularly dazzled by this legislation. I do not think it will do much good. It certainly will not do any harm. I think the agreement we reached to pass this bill by ten o'clock tonight is very good.

subtopic: FARM IMPROVEMENT, SMALL BUSINESSES AND FISHERIES IMPROVEMENT LOANS ACT AMENDMENTS RESPECTING LOANS AND GOVERNMENT LIABILITY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is indeed a pleasure for me to join other hon. members in this debate on Bill C-14. This bill introduced by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Turner) does one basic thing: it raises the maximum of ceiling on the amount of money that chartered banks in this country can loan to small businesses. This includes loans to fishermen and farmers for improvement and possible enlargement of their respective enterprises.
I welcome this piece of legislation because it appears to be one of those rare occasions when this government recognizes the need for assistance and attention to these important segments of our economy. Small business establishments are, without question, the very lifeblood and backbone of our communities, our provinces and indeed our country. I am deeply concerned that so little consideration has been given to such an important group who not only individually but collectively contribute so much to our economy and social well-being. I have tremendous respect for these businessmen and businesswomen. Upon investigation, you will find the best managerial skill, the greatest efficiency and real determination, dedication and initiative in this group. Most of these people established their businesses over the years, not with government assistance or grants but with faith in their communities, faith in themselves, faith in their country-and few dollars.
My main criticism of this bill-and I am certain it is a criticism shared by many other hon. members-is that the ceilings, although increased, are still far too low and unrealistic. They are unrealistic, Mr. Speaker, when you take into account the serious financial difficulties being experienced in these areas and the tremendous increases in the price of production equipment, buildings and machinery. Small businessmen in Ontario, as well as elsewhere in Canada, in part because of present government

programs, have been increasingly discouraged from investing, expanding and establishing new enterprises. In many cases, taxation policies have encouraged businessmen to pull up stakes rather than solidify or enlarge their base of operation. Small businesses particularly have been looking to government to provide the help and incentives to not only compete but to grow and thrive. When one examines the bankruptcies and rapidly dwindling numbers employed in these segments of our economy, it becomes apparent that government action has been lacking and is greatly needed now.
If we read the minister's press release on these three loan acts dated Wednesday, November 21, 1973, we note that the Small Businesses Loans Act which came into effect in January, 1961, lent from that time until September, 1973, approximately $283 million. This appears to be a lot of money, and indeed it is. However, upon looking a little closer we find that about the same amount was lent this year as was lent last year, that is, about $15.5 million. Fewer loans were granted. Indeed, quite an insignificant number of the 268 loans made between April and September of 1973 went to the province of Ontario. The Fisheries Improvement Loans Act which came into effect December, 1955, has lent from that date to the end of September, 1973, $29.5 million. Since the amount of money lent nearly doubled from $2.5 million to $4 million during the April to September period from 1972 to 1973, it would appear that this program more adequately meets the financial requirements of the fishing industry than it does small businesses.
One begins to wonder just how useful the program is when no loans were granted in five of Canada's ten provinces and total loans granted amount to only 577. The province of Ontario, which has a sizeable inland fishing business involving nearly 2,000 people and some 106 million pounds valued at $13.5 million, was granted only eight loans. In fact, the inland fishing industry experienced a 12 per cent decrease in volume of catch and a 7 per cent decrease in value of stocks taken in 1970 over 1969.
The $50,000 ceiling place on the Fisheries Improvement Loans Act by Bill C-14 is unrealistic by today's standards. Fishermen are a breed of their own. I am certain that my friends in this House representing ridings in the Atlantic and Pacific regions would agree. I have the pleasure of representing some of these fishermen in the Lake Erie area of Port Stanley and Port Burwell. Fishermen are a hardy group. They are hard working and are willing to risk their lives in the everyday pursuit of their duties in order to provide food for Canadians and to secure a very modest income for themselves and their families. They, too, have experienced increased input costs in their industry for boats, diesel engines, buildings, refrigeration and other equipment necessary for continued operation of their business enterprises.
When we study the performance of the Farm Improvement Loans Act we find that significantly more loans were granted and considerably more money was lent. Since its inception in March, 1945, until the end of September, 1973, nearly $3 billion has been lent and a marked increase is noted, from $105.5 million in 1972 to $125 million in 1973 during the April to September periods. However, about the same number of loans were granted during
Loans Acts Amendments
the year 1972-73. The real information that is lacking from all three of these government programs is the total number of applications and inquiries made to the chartered banks and the number refused for various reasons. I would be willing to admit that some of the applications were rejected for good reason, but this information should be available if we are to develop the kinds of programs and policies that will best meet the needs and financial requirements of these industries.
It is a well known fact that people, and in particular young people, are leaving these segments of our economy. Most noticeable are those leaving the fishery and farming areas. I am sure that, along with other reasons, this is the result of the difficulty they encounter in securing the capital necessary to enter or continue these businesses. It is true that to some extent the shortcomings in loan programs have in recent times been remedied by amendments to the Farm Credit Corporation Act.
I welcome the fact that small businesses are now defined as businesses worth up to $1 million. No doubt the current rate of inflation played its part in the consideration leading to this decision. I am reminded in this connection of a remark of my hon. friend from Mackenzie (Mr. Korchinski), "Thank God for inflation: we shall all be millionaires!" A number of sound recommendations were made in the brief of the Canadian Federation of Agriculture presented to the cabinet and to opposition parties. Realising the need for an increase in the ceiling level, the federation recommended a maximum of $50,000 in respect of farm machinery and land, and a total maximum of $100,000. In my opinion, this is certainly in order. Taking into account the fact that a similar situation confronts both the fishing industry and those engaged in small business enterprises, I submit that if Bill C-14 is to have any effective impact, corresponding increases should be made in amounts available under the programs designed to assist small businesses and the fishing industry.

subtopic: FARM IMPROVEMENT, SMALL BUSINESSES AND FISHERIES IMPROVEMENT LOANS ACT AMENDMENTS RESPECTING LOANS AND GOVERNMENT LIABILITY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to be able to speak on Bill C-14 for a few minutes toward the close of this debate. I am sure the fact that I introduced a private member's motion on January 22 of last year, shortly after the opening of the session, asking that the ceiling under this legislation be increased from $25,000 to $75,000 in no way influenced the government in reaching its decision. I am pleased to find, however, that the government is only 15 months behind the thinking of the people of Hastings county.
The idea of an omnibus bill is probably a good one. I should like to say two things with regard to the portion which deals with loans for farm improvement. Specific allowance is made, now, for those acquiring new businesses, but I should like to point out that no one can start in the farming business with $50,000. In fact, a man cannot start in southern Ontario with $100,000; he probably needs $150,000.
Second, there is a crying need to revise our conception of the term "farmer". Some provision ought to be made to enable a young man to work at a job which provides cash for his everyday necessities while still operating a farm. Surprisingly enough, despite all the criticism of young

April 11, 1974
Loans Acts Amendments
people which we hear today, there are still many in my area who are prepared to work at jobs which provide the dollars indispensable for their daily needs while preparing for a future on the farm. They wish to be farmers, and I think the rules ought to be changed to make this possible.
I propose to devote the remainder of my remarks, in the limited time available to me, strictly to the small business aspect of the legislation before us. The reasons for the amendment are more valid today than they have ever been. Since 1961, when the legislative machinery was first set up, costs have risen to such an extent that it is not sufficient to substitute a ceiling of $50,000 for $25,000. What piece of construction equipment can a man entering the construction business buy for $25,000? If he is engaged in manufacturing, raw materials alone would cost in the neighbourhood of $50,000. In the wholesale business one can hardly get a decent stock of cigarettes and chocolate bars for less than $50,000. Take transport: with the big highway rigs it costs more than $30,000 for the tractor alone, quite apart from the trailer. So there is very little one can do with $50,000 in the way of starting a small business in Canada these days.
The Industrial Development Bank, which supposedly should be looking after these areas of concern, has not been doing its job. I have spoken at some length on this subject on other occasions. The intention was that it should lend in areas of high risk at a somewhat higher interest rate. Well, they charge the high interest rate but they rarely get into the high risk area. As a result, businessmen have to rely on legislation such as we see before us.
I am pleased it should now be possible to buy land under these provisions. I am interested in finding out how this section will work, because it will really amount to a form of mortgage and with interest rates as they are today I am curious to know what arrangements will be made with the first person who borrows money under these terms. I am pleased that new businesses are now covered. These are changes which are beneficial. The Small Businesses Loans Act was intended to be of help to businessmen. The increase in the loans ceilings and in the size of eligible companies constitutes an advance, but the government has not gone far enough. While we are disposed to pass the bill, I urge the ministers concerned to reconsider these measures in the near future.
Mr. Speaker, I see it is close to five o'clock, and since I know we wish to move forward I will resume my seat.
Motion agreed to, bill read the second time and the House went into committee thereon, Mr. Boulanger in the chair.

speechtext:
Mr. Jack Marshall (Humber-St. George's-St. Barbe moved:
That an order of the House do issue for a copy of all material resulting from the first meeting of the VLA senior management team convened by the Director General of the Veterans Land Administration in Ottawa from March 26 to 29 as follows (a) operational plans in the periods before and after the March 31, 1974 deadline for new loan applications (b) further implementation of MBO as the VLA style of management.
He said: Mr. Speaker, there must be something radically wrong here.
This is the second time I have risen to my feet-I think that is the first time it has happened in six years-to speak twice on the same day. At least not everybody has gone home.
I missed one thing when I was talking on the Fisheries Improvement Loans measure. The hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) reminded me of it. He said I should have asked the Minister of Finance (Mr. Turner) whether he would increase the maximum loan ceilings under the Veterans Land Act to $50,000.
The debate today is the result of my notice of motion for the production of papers requesting a copy of all material resulting from the first meeting of the Veterans Land Act senior management team which was convened by the Director General of the Veterans Land Administration in Ottawa from March 26 to March 29, and also the operational plans in the periods before and after the March 31, 1974 deadline for new loan applications, and in respect of fur-
April 11, 1974

ther implementation of MBO, whatever that is, as the VLA style of management.
It is very difficult for ,ne to understand why the production of these papers was denied. It is a well-known fact that as a result of a notice of motion introduced by an hon. member of this party the government, even though it was reluctant to recognize the wishes of the majority of veterans, said it was prepared to phase out certain parts of the veterans' charter on the basis of the fact that nine years ago, in 1965, the parliament of Canada agreed that it should be phased out. My only comment in that regard is: so what? I should like to ask members of the House how many amendments to legislation have come about over the years, and how many changes have had to be made because of changing conditions?
I am sure the members of the House of Commons who were here in 1965, and agreed with the decision to establish deadline dates, now realize that this was a wrong decision. Is that not why we are sitting here in the House of Commons as members? We are sitting here to legislate, and to change legislation for the benefit of the people we represent. To use an argument such as the one used by members on the other side of this House is ridiculous and even un-Canadian.
In dealing with this motion for the production of papers,
I think it was yesterday I was told by the minister that since the papers for which I asked were confidential documents they should not be produced. I wonder how ridiculous that is, and what was so confidential at the meeting of the Veterans Land Act Administration that we, as members of parliament, should be denied the right to know the operational plans for the period before and after the March 31 deadline for new loan applications, and in respect of further implementation of MBO as the Veterans Land Act style of management?
Now that the government has extended the March 31, 1974, deadline is it not that much more important that veterans know about the operational plans of this administration? That seems only to be commonsense. This debate allows me to place on the record the attitude which has been taken by government members opposite in respect of extending the deadline for one year.
During a TV program last week the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) was asked about the vast increase in government expenditure, and gave as an excuse the fact that the extension of the VLA deadline had contributed to this increase in government expenditure. Let me refer to the transcript which indicates that the Prime Minister, in response to a question, said that just last week the government was trying to phase out a program for veterans which had been brought in after the second world war, and applicable to the Korean veterans, according to a schedule determined many years ago by parliament, but when the government acted on phasing it out people said it should be prolonged for another year.
The Prime Minister went on to say that another reason was the result of pressure groups supported by the opposition, and he added that by extending the program it would cost several millions of dollars. Another misconception which should be corrected was in relation to a statement made by one of the newsmen that there are 10,000 civil servants in this department. There may be 10,000 civil
Veterans Land Administration servants in the entire Department of Veterans Affairs, but there are fewer than 500 administering the Veterans Land Act.
Having regard to the pressure groups referred to by the Prime Minister, this used to be referred to as involvement and participation by the people of Canada. Now these have become pressure groups. When it suited the government to invite Canadians to get involved in government, this was known as involvement and participation, but now these people are "pressure groups supported by the opposition".
Let me take a few moments to answer the questions about the cost of operating the Veterans Land Act administration. The best way I can do that is by reading from questions and answers reported in the Proceedings and Evidence of the Standing Committee on Veterans Affairs, Issue No. 4 for April 4, 1974. I said:
-I would like to go on to the estimates. I think I was questioning Mr. McCracken about the budget, and I hear certain figures bandied around. I want to clarify in my own mind and in the mind of the Committee, the Veterans' Land Administration expenditures for the operation of the Veterans' Land Administration Program. Am I correct in assuming that the amount in the estimates is $11,570,423?
Mr. McCracken answered as follows:
Yes, Mr. Chairman. That includes an amount of about $4,400,000 which is a reserve that is set aside every year to meet the conditional grant benefit of the loans that are made to veterans, so that at the end of 10 years, there is an amount available from this reserve in the case of a veteran, for instance, who has a small holding loan.
He has a $1,400 conditional grant of the first $6,000. At the end of 10 years when he has fulfilled the terms of his settlement contract, $1,400 is taken from the reserve and it is applied in effect to his debt. So of the 11 million and some odd dollars, $4.4 million of that is an amount that is set aside and it remains fairly constant... It is set aside each year to build up this reserve so that we can write off the conditional grants at the end of the 10-year period.
I then asked:
So, in other words, the cost of operating a department is not $11 million, it is more like $7 million.
His answer to that was:
The actual operating costs per se are about $7.2 million, yes.
I then asked:
-if the deadline in the Veterans Land Act was not extended, you indicated at the last Committee meeting that the Veterans' Land Administration would remain intact at least until 1977, and you went on to say there would have to be some semblance of a Veterans' Land Administration in the year 2000.
In other words the Veterans' Land Administration would not be phased out even if the deadline had not been extended. Mr. McCracken went on to say:
There would have to be staff somewhere and I conceive it remaining as a unit whether it was in the Department of Veterans Affairs or some other department, where the staff involved would be handling the loan management workload, the agreements of sale, conveyances and this type of thing. The people and the staff in the regions would be there in regard to matters of collections and this type of thing. Loan management workload is the name we normally give to it.
I then asked:
In other words, even if the extension of a year was not imposed or agreed upon or brought in, that staff would still remain and the cost would be the same?
Mr. McCracken replied:
Some staff, yes. I envisage that in about three years' time, we would be down from about 490 now to around the 400 mark.

April 11, 1974
Veterans Land Administration
Let us then correct the misconception that there are
10,000	civil servants operating the Veterans' Land Administration, as there is a staff of less than 500 which will be down to 400 by the end of the year. I then asked Mr. McCracken:
Therefore, from what I can see there would be no great increase in cost to maintain the present staff to take care of the extension of the deadline for a year; there would be no undue, unreasonable cost to the public.
Mr. McCracken said:
Well, I am not going to comment on the question of whether it is undue or otherwise. I can say this: that relating to the amount we have in the estimates for 1974-75, I anticipate an additional requirement of not less than $1 million this year.
In other words, to satisfy what they suggest will be another 10,000 veterans by extending the deadline by one year, this will cost $1 million. So let us correct that misconception. I then asked Mr. McCracken:
For what reason?
Mr. McCracken said:
Increased operating costs.
To confirm that again I asked:
It would be just $1 million?
Mr. McCracken replied:
A minimum of $1 million.
Then the deputy minister said:
Mr. Chairman, may I interject? The estimates were prepared on the assumption that the act, as it then stood, would continue to apply. That is to say that during the fiscal year that has just begun, loans would not be made. Since the act has been amended, As Mr. McCracken said, there is an additional expense involved.
Certainly there is an additional expense involved, but it is only $1 million and not the many millions quoted by the minister, the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau), and many others who do not know what they are talking about. I then asked this:
Mr. McCracken, in the short time since the legislation was passed, have you had any information from your district authorities indicating that there is an influx of applications?
He said he did not because he did not think there was enough time.
Then I asked him if he was getting a rush because the deadline was approaching, and he said that that would be putting it mildly. I said:
It has been indicated by the department or Veterans' Land Administration that of the 140,000 veterans qualified only between 5 and 10 per cent would seek applications under the act. Up to the March 31, 1974 deadline, has that proven true?
Then Mr. McCracken said:
Mr. Chairman, I think that would be about right. Since October 1968, new establishments have been running around 3,000. I think we hit 4,000 in 1968-69, if my memory serves me correctly, but it has been running around 3,000 to 4,000. This year the number of loans actually approved for veterans who were seeking establishment, exclusive of the backlog we have, would be around 5,500. That would work out to around the 20,000 mark, somewhere in that area.
Just because there was agreement nine years ago in this House of Commons that the deadline would be established does not preclude the possibility that it was the wrong

decision to make. Since the nine years have passed the facts are clear, and the chairman of the Veterans' Land Act administration, an honourable and very capable man, has told us what the situation is. We have performed a service for at least a few thousand veterans over the next year who will be able to take advantage of the legislation. Let me say once more that it will not cost the millions of dollars mentioned, but rather $1 million.
The staff will be in existence at least until 1977, so the necessary staff will be available either through the Department of Veterans Affairs or through some other department up until the year 2000. I do not know where the suggested heavy expenditure comes from, because it certainly will not be due to the extension of the deadline. I think it could be shown in respect of a cost-benefit analysis of the value of any government agency that the VLA is as good an example as any of proper government spending.
There are many other areas in which spending could be cut but not in the area of the veterans charter. In order to show the type of amendments my party suggests-and in this I include the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles)-I should like to refer to a motion I introduced before the committee, which for some reason or other was not acceptable. This amendment stated:
That this Committee recommends the government consider the advisability of introducing legislation to provide:
1.	That Section 31 of the Veterans Land Act be repealed;
2.	That the mortgage loan ceiling be increased to $30,000 from the present $18,000 to meet realistically today's needs;
3.	That the minimum lot requirement be reduced from the present one-half acre less 20 per cent, or 17,424 square feet, to a lot commensurate with CMHC requirements, for those veterans desirous of acquiring building lots in urban areas;
4.	That the down payment be equated to 5 per cent of the loan ceiling; and the Chairman be instructed to report this recommendation to the House later this day.
For some reason or other my motion was not considered correct and was turned down. However, the government and everybody here know that these factors I have mentioned are consistent with the extension of the deadline. We will continue to press for this over the next 12 months. I am sure all members on the other side now realize this is the only justifiable and proper thing to do for the veterans.
When we introduce a motion in a new form I hope these amendments will receive approval, and will not be considered out of order under the rules of the House. In the meantime my motion for the production of papers should be answered, and the papers should be produced so that what the veterans administration management team does will be within the knowledge of each member of this House who has veterans in his district, and who represents veterans' organizations, so that those veterans may be helped rather than kept in the dark as they have been for so long.

subsubtopic: MATERIAL RESULTING FROM FIRST MEETING OF VLA SENIOR MANAGEMENT TEAM MARCH 26-29, 1974
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this motion for the production of papers put by the hon. member for Humber-St. George's-St. Barbe (Mr. Marshall) gives us another opportunity to bring new matter to the continuing debate on the veterans' land program.
April 11, 1974

We had several occasions, Mr. Speaker, to consider the requests, perhaps legitimate requests of certains veterans associations concerning the extention of the implementation period of the program announced in 1942, to provide veterans returning from the front mortgages at easier terms than those offered in 1945.
As was said before, Mr. Speaker, the spirit prevailing at the time was to provide veterans with a mortgage market which was non-exiting from 1945 to 1952 and greatly different from the present market where, as soon as a worker gets a steady job, he can apply to the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation and benefit from a very advantageous mortgage program well known throughout Canada. This enabled the government to have construction started on no fewer than 260,000 housing units in 1973.
This debate, Mr. Speaker, gives us nonetheless the opportunity to refute some points raised only a few minutes ago by the hon. member for Humber-St. George's-St. Barbe (Mr. Marshall), when speaking of the cost of the amendment he wished to move in committee. Therefore, since he has opened the debate on what happened in that committee, I will also take leave, Mr. Speaker, to discuss the proposed amendment.
The hon. member talked of a cost of $1 million and has quoted at length from the proceedings of the April 4 meeting and he quoted Mr. McCracken as having said that the extention of the program would cost about $1 million only, that is to say what it would cost to keep a staff of 490 and carry on other obligations.
But to be honest, I must say that this sum of $1 million does not include the requested benefits. If the ceiling of mortgage loans were raised from $18,000 to $30,000, it is quite sure, as one can figure out by very simple calculations, that such a program would not be possible with only $1 million.
Besides, one has to consider that as many as 110,000 veterans have a certificate and that they could probably use if it the benefits were increased from $18,000 to $30,000.
Then, after calculations, we must conclude that since 1967 approximately 20,000 veterans took advantage of the government's proposal, of whom 99 per cent are said to have first chosen the settlement or university training programs.
They have repaid what they had already received from the government to accept the offer made to them in 1967. Some 110,000 have done this since 1968 and no fewer than
20,000	have used their certificate to take advantage of the veterans' land program.
Of course, if the ceiling were fixed at $30,000 rather than $18,000, it is most certain that a great number of the remaining 110,000 would come to the Veterans Affairs Department to benefit from this program.
Anybody who will try to convince me that this kind of program would cost no more than $1 million yearly cannot be taken seriously, because he is not good at figures. As to the administration costs, and I am sure the hon. member agrees on this, they would be of about $1 million, according to Mr. McCracken, director of the program. But if the ceiling were to be raised, program costs would greatly exceed $1 million; indeed, a figure of $50 million has been
Veterans Land Administration
suggested. I am not in a position, Mr. Speaker, to see whether that $50 million is correct, but I trust those who figured it out and consider that it could in fact cost as much as $50 million.
Another point I should like to raise in this debate, Mr. Speaker, is that certain innuendoes were made in this House and elsewhere that about March 12, the hon. member for Edmonton West (Mr. Lambert) said, and I quote:
... I have heard reports from some of them that they are finding an extraordinary working-to-rule in some VLA offices with regard to this matter.
He went on:
I hope those reports are wrong, because I think this House would severely castigate any officials of VLA who in any way dragged their feet in order to have this deadline pass and applications thus disqualified.
And later on, Mr. Speaker, on March 28, similar allegations were made in committee by another hon. member, namely that it was rumoured that the staff was still working to rule in receiving and processing applications. Mr. Speaker, there could not be anything more untrue than such allegations. I am told by the administrator of the program that the 490 persons working in the Veterans' Land Act administration are honest civil servants, honest employees of the department. The great majority, 75 per cent of the employees, are veterans themselves, and about 100 per cent of them are male employees. Mr. Speaker, to give you an example of their dedications to their work, I should quote the words spoken on March 23 by Mr. McCracken, which are published on page 114 of the committee proceedings, and I quote:
In a management decision last year, we agreed that in the months of January, February and March of this year there would be no holidays for field staff, district managers, and others so that we would have a full complement of staff available to take care of the anticipated increase in loan applications that we would receive in that period. We anticipated that we would have an increase in the number of veterans who would be coming in for counselling purposes.

In my opinion, Mr. Speaker, this intention and these steps taken by department officials to ensure that all applications would be considered in time to meet the deadline of March 31, 1974, clearly demonstrate that there had been absolutely no decline in effectiveness of department employees who did not even hesitate to sacrifice their winter holiday to which they were duly entitled to ensure that all veterans' applications would be processed in time.
This is another statement which causes us to question the seriousness of those who came forward with these figures, statements and unfounded information.
The minister was even accused of not having done the utmost to contact all Canadian veterans so that they could take advantage of the benefits made available to them.
Mr. Speaker, in 1967, Mr. McCracken fully explained all the measures that had been taken that year and gave them intensive publicity, mainly in the newspapers, for the sake of the veterans. For instance, in the Canadian Legion

April 11, 1974
Veterans Land Administration
bulletin and in all the veterans newspapers. Posters have been displayed in many Canadian legions across the country, in post offices, in public places familiar to the veterans to inform them of the new provisions, the extension date of the applicability of the act which they were granted and the new provisions covering the extension of their benefits. As a consequence, Mr. Speaker, no fewer than
140,000	veterans took advantage of this offer and reimbursed the benefits they had already received to obtain the new publicized ones.
So, how far do we have to go? In Europe, and in France, for example, in early June every year they celebrate the liberation anniversary date, and so will they this year. In early June, they celebrate Europe's liberation by the allied nations.
This year European countries, and especially France, decided that after 30 years it would be proper to commemorate in a special way that 30th anniversary of the liberation of Europe but that in later years that event would be much less important for the good reason that after 30 years it is becoming more and more difficult for veterans to participate in the commemoration of that major event in our history and especially that of Europe.
When one considers that veterans are 58 or 59 on the average, naturally, it is becoming more and more difficult for them to go back to the battle fields and recall the difficult hours they went through 30 years ago.
It is not any easier, Mr. Speaker, for a man of that age to make plans and I say so as a man who discussed this with his former brothers-in-arms. Since I too attend quite regularly the meetings of my local Canadian Legion I am in constant touch with veterans who agree with me and say: Well, listen, after so many years those who wanted to go into farming, those who wanted to settle have already done so, and at our age-58 or 59 on the average-it has become quite difficult to make such plans.
For those reasons, Mr. Speaker, the government decided to extend the provisions of the Veterans' Land Act for another year. New facts might prompt the government to extend that cutoff date. Mr. Speaker, the motion for the production of papers now before the House once again gives us an opportunity to review the legislation to which it pertains. We have heard the mover of the motion suggest the amendments that he would look for, and several of us, speaking previously on the same subject, which seems to be repeating itself so many times in this session, have suggested that the legislation should have been phased out long since and, if necessary, different legislation introduced for our veterans. However, in order that we may make an assessment before voting on this motion it may be well to review the subject. I think it would be relevant to quote the following parts of the preamble to the act:
Whereas many men now serving in the active forces of Canada have recorded their desire to settle on land or engage in farming when

hostilities cease, and it is desirable that suitably qualified veterans be encouraged to seek rehabilitation in the agricultural industry;
And whereas part time farming coupled with other employment is an increasingly important aspect of rural and semi-rural life in Canada;
And whereas it is in the public interest as a measure of rehabilitation to assist in acquiring the ownership of farm homes by qualified veterans-
In relation to the purpose of assisting to rehabilitate veterans in civilian life, as hon. members know every veteran has had at least 20 years to make his application, and most have had as long as 30 years. The other two alternative rehabilitation plans were concluded quite some time ago. I think it is clear that the orientation of the Veterans Land Act was directed principally to those veterans interested in agricultural utilization of farm land in rural and semi-rural areas. The financial provisions of the act were founded on this type of settlement, and I think we should not lose sight of those basic factors when we discuss the act.
When we look at some of the facts we see that in the eight fiscal years up to March, 1973, after the lending deadlines and revised loan ceilings were established in 1965, approximately 32,000 veterans were settled under the provisions of the act. In the majority of those eight years the annual number of new establishments has been less than 5,000. In the current fiscal year, however, and more particularly in the last six months, there has been a significant increase in the number of loan applications. It is expected that the number of veterans who will have been settled this year will approximate 5,500-and there are a further 1,400 loan applications on hand awaiting appraisal.
It was in the light of this data on comparative settlement activity and the increased interest which veterans have shown in the current fiscal year-due undoubtedly to recognition by them of the scheduled lending deadline- that I reached the conclusion that an extension of one year, as has been approved by the minister, would be appropriate. In my analysis of the facts it became evident that some well-intentioned veterans would have been deprived of a right, which they had so gallantly earned, if the March, 1974, deadline had been final.
When there is a reasonable doubt, we should not hesitate to decide in favour of the veterans. We must not forget that, some years ago, they did not hesitate when the survival of freedom was in doubt. The extension that has been granted will provide many veterans with an opportunity to take advantage of a program which was designed for them.
The Veterans Land Act was designed neither as a program of urban housing nor as part of a retirement program for persons reaching the end of their productive careers. Its basic purpose was to provide loans for the purchase of agricultural land, to be used on a full or part time farming basis by veterans who were interested in this form of rehabilitation program on their return to civilian life following wartime active service.
It was recognized that many veterans would neither wish nor find it practical to settle under the Veterans Land Act. Two other programs were enacted: university training under the Veterans Rehabilitation Act, and reestablishment credits under the War Service Grants Act. The benefits under all three programs were alternative
April 11, 1974

one to the other. Each veteran had the right to choose whichever plan he considered would best serve his needs and desires.
The department's university training program was concluded in the 1950s; and October 31, 1968, was the final date for veterans to use re-establishment credit benefits.
In 1965 parliament established deadlines to phase out VLA lending operations in a reasonable and orderly manner. Almost 30 years have elapsed since the end of World War II, and 20 years in the case of the Korean conflict. In the context of a rehabilitation measure to assist veterans to pick up the thread of civilian life following wartime active service, those genuinely interested in land settlement assistance have had ample time to find properties suitable for this purpose.
Mr. Speaker, there have been suggestions, by hon. members reading such implications into the motion, that possibly the government's concern for veterans is lessening. Surely nothing could be rurther from the truth.

I think the problem is that in spending many days debating the Veterans Land Act we have been using the poor veterans for our political purposes and motives. We have done that instead of coming to grips with the question and recognizing that, possibly at this late date, veterans legislation should be introduced to take care of veterans now reaching retirement age. I feel, because of their service to their country, that there should be programs in which they can participate which will enable them to settle in retirement with benefits somewhat above those available to the average citizen.
This is a debatable point. The consensus of opinion seems to be that a little more should be given to the veteran in view of the service he has performed for his country. I do not oppose that. We are calling for these extensions to an act which should long since have been phased out. The allegation which is made that by calling
Veterans Land Administration for the conclusion of the act we shall do something which is against the interests of veterans is hypocritical. We should face the issue. In lieu of inadequate legislation we should introduce legislation that we feel is necessary and which will benefit veterans who are now reaching retirement age.
I feel that the motion before the House, like all similar motions, is the type of probing motion designed to make public confidential departmental papers. Mr. Chairman, I should like to make a few brief comments about this bill. There is no doubt that there is need for the extension of greater credit in the farming community and in the small business community, and this has been caused by inflation, as stated a few minutes ago by the hon. member for Don Valley.
During meetings of the Standing Committee on Agriculture we discussed this matter with representatives of the Federation of Agriculture, at which time everyone seemed to agree that because of the increase in prices there was a need to increase the limitation in respect of the amount of loans available. It was generally agreed that $15,000 was a ridiculously low figure, and that credit to the extent of at least $25,000 must be made available to farmers to cover production costs as well as the cost of machinery. Hon. members will realize that the price of machinery has been skyrocketing in the past few years, and it is generally understood that the cost will go up another 25 per cent in the next year. This is horrifying to the farmers.
During our discussions about this matter I ventured to state, with tongue in cheek, that as a result of inflation we will soon all be millionaires. This is exactly what will happen within a very few years. None of us will be worth any more or own any more property, but perhaps we will all be millionaires. This puts me in mind of stories about the people in Germany having to push a wheelbarrow full of marcs to the store to purchase a loaf of bread. That is the point we are rapidly moving toward at this present rate of inflation.
Because the land a man might have purchased in the 1930's for $500 would now cost $25,000 many people seem to think that all farmers are rich. Let me point out that the same acre of land produces no more food. Perhaps I should correct that by admitting that greater production is now possible through the use of fertilizers that were not available in the 1930's. We are able to produce a few more bushels of crop per acre, but this increased production is soon gobbled up.
April 11, 1974

In my experience I have never met a farmer who has purchased his machinery with cash. I was the reeve in a municipality for about six years, I am in my seventeenth year as a member of this House, and I can honestly tell hon. members that I know of not one farmer who has purchased machinery with cash. They have always had to go to the bank first to make arrangements for the money. Perhaps they do not do this because they want to, but it seems that savings are a thing of the past nowadays. I think the younger generation has the right idea; that is, use somebody else's money and live off the fat of the land. This is what causes the inflation. I believe there is a need for this type of loan for those who are left on the farm and who provide the needs of this country and other countries.
The minister has been making some strange noises in the last couple of days. He has been suggesting that if the farmers wish to be treated like everybody else they should pay high interest rates such as 10 per cent or 12 per cent. I am referring to the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan), not the Minister of Finance (Mr. Turner).

Mr. Chairman, I am particularly interested in the agricultural aspect of this, so I was not really reflecting on the Minister of Finance. The Minister of Agriculture has been listening to the debate, but it would seem that all he got out of it is the fact that horsepower has increased in farm machinery and that larger equipment is necessary. Surely he has missed the whole point, Mr. Chairman. The reason farmers have to buy bigger farm equipment is because they cannot make a living off the land these days the way they could 20 years ago, and so they have had to expand.
The minister indicated that more fertilizer will be used this year, but he must know that that is not necessarily so. Less than the optimum amount of fertilizer will probably be used because it is so expensive. In order to get satisfactory results in Canada, fertilizer should be applied for a number of years. This has not happened, so the maximum production cannot be achieved.
The minister must be aware that the input to agriculture has been higher than ever before. Every time there is an increase in price he finds himself faced with expenditures beyond those he had anticipated.
A good example of this is the changes that took place in the Ontario dairy industry. As soon as farmers were able to enter the industrial milk market where there was a guaranteed price, they had to buy bulk tanks and a new type of milking machine. They also had to upgrade their buildings. Usually they had to get a loan, which ate up any profit from the expanded operation.

I hope the minister is not as satisfied as he appears to be that there is no problem in the farm machinery industry. I hope he is not satisfied that there is no problem in the fertilizer industry. I hope he is not satisfied that there is no problem in the binder twine industry, the fencing industry, to say nothing of the basic problem that faces all farmers, the cost of land. Whether it is purchased outright, or through ARDA, or rented, it is still expensive. I hope the minister is not satisfied that the inputs have to be left alone and that, if we pass this legislation, a satisfactory solution has been found for agricultural producers.
I have found that farmers are in almost the same category as workers, Mr. Chairman. When the cost of production rises or the worker's cost of living rises, then either his standard has to be reduced or his production has to be reduced. The farmer has to curtail either his production or standard of living, or he has to borrow more money.
I suggest that the problem is not so much one for the Minister of Finance as it is for the Minister of Agriculture. The Minister of Fisheries should also be involved, I think, and so should the minister responsible for small businesses. The reason the Minister of Finance is being asked for this kind of legislation, and the reason the government is answering the call of the farmer, the small businessman, and the fisherman to increase the amounts of the loans, is that in order to stay in business these people must modernize; they must put more in to get more out.
As production costs increase we must raise lending ceilings to enable farmers to keep up and extend production. It is the case with almost every commodity, but whereas farmers have increased their production, their returns have decreased. Take the case of grain, a matter with which I am not overly familiar. The western farmer found that the price of his product rose almost overnight from $1.95 to about $6.00; yet the futures market in the last two or three months has dropped $1.50. If the farmer operates in a totally uncontrolled free enterprise market, he must consider carefully any move to increase production because, unless the government guarantees a floor price for his product, he may find that he is overproducing, that his return has decreased, but his expenses have not been reduced in line with his decreased return.
I am sure the minister does not really believe that it is enough to provide extended financing to farmers to enable them to expand their operation. He does not believe, I am sure, that farmers across Canada are using enough fertilizer. I am sure he knows that many farmers growing wheat in western Canada were only able to keep production costs down by using less than the optimum amount of fertilizer. I am also sure he knows that many farmers who grew corn in his area and sold it for reasonable prices were not applying adequate fertilizer.
In addition, I am sure he knows that although one segment of the farm industry has grown, and although it could be claimed that the price per horsepower of machinery has not increased significantly, this does not correct matters.
The government has advocated, in the last five or six years, the acquisition of larger farm units. It has suggested that we need to develop viable agricultural farm units.

This has meant that the farmer has had to buy his neighbour's farm. He has bought more land and expanded. Because he has expanded he has had to increase the machinery horsepower at his disposal. Unless the minister pays attention to methods of reducing input costs he will be doing the farmer a disservice. Only in that way can we strike a reasonable balance between the price at the farm gate and the price to the consumer. If we do not lower input c$>sts, which include the cost of borrowing money, we will not have served well the farmers of this country.

Mr. Chairman, I just want to make a few general comments. This will allow the minister to relax somewhat because I will not be confronting him with direct questions. Anyway I do not think he would be ready this evening to implement the suggestions I will be making to help farmers and small businessmen in Canada.
I am one of that group who grew up in the small business world. I even have a small farm. It is big in land mass, but small in turnover and profit. I became a politician through the many experiences I gathered going to the bank and convincing my banker that he should make me another loan.
It usually happens in this way. You have an idea. You think it is great. You think it is going to make you rich. You go to your banker and tell him it will cost $15,000 to get you going. Your name is pretty good and your face looks alright, so the banker says he has the authority to loan you $15,000. Three months later you go back to the bank and tell your banker that if he wants his $15,000, you need another $25,000 because that is what you need to make this thing really viable.
The banker phones the regional office in a distant city and gets the approval to loan you another $25,000. Usually a small business makes a profit after the first year. This is contrary to big business. They do not make profits for generations.
In April of the following year, the small businessman invariably goes to the bank to borrow money to pay his income tax. He then wonders where all the profits went. At that time the bank knows the chances of success. The banker then decides whether you should close your doors or whether he should loan you the additional money.
I started quite a few small businesses. A lot of them are still going. In fact, some of them are now big. I ended up with very little for my share. Most of them were pretty sensible and pretty successful. I have analysed some of the programs the government has for helping small businessmen and farmers. I wonder about the reasons for some of these programs, and whether these people would not be better served with other programs that would make more sense.
Earlier this year I listened to the Minister of Agriculture talk about the farm succession legislation. In order to preserve the family farm he wanted to be sure that the poor son taking over the farm did not have to pay income tax on the capital investment. When I listened to the minister I wondered whether the act was designed to preserve the family farm or to expedite the death of the farmer.
The Farm Improvement Loans Act and the Farm Credit Act are wonderful. I want to congratulate the minister for making the Farm Improvement Loans Act more sensible, more in tune with our time, more in tune with inflation, and a little more meaningful. I am certainly in favour of it. It is all we have to work with. However, I wonder whether it would not better serve these people if the act, more ambitiously and in a more meaningful way, provided farmers with a means of getting their product to market.

Farmers do not like big statistics tables. They use practical statistics. I came across a statistic the other day which stated that 20 per cent less boxcars were loaded in Canada in 1973 than in 1972, and that in 1973 the production of alcohol in Canada went up by 15 per cent. That proves only one thing: There were more people loaded in Canada last year than there were boxcars! Did I miss something?

speechtext:
Was it 5 per cent? It does not make that much difference. I think we would be better served if our government would provide us with transportation facilities to get our products to market, and storage facilities whereby we could store a year's production of grain.
I learned that in small business you cannot sell from an empty shelf. That is what the marketers have been doing in Canada. When they travel around the world they either sell from an empty shelf or one that is running over. Either they have nothing to sell, or they have to sell at firesale prices to get rid of the production because there is no place to store it.
Instead of all these so-called subsidies, we would be better off if the government provided us with a transportation system. We would also be better served if the government would recognize the need for a proper place for the farmer to sell his product. By that I mean that sooner or later the farmer will have to get paid for what he produces and he will have to get paid a decent price.
Many of my colleagues have touched on statistics regarding other parts of the world. They have pointed out that some people have to pay up to 50 per cent of their disposable income for food, whereas in Canada we pay less than 20 per cent. The time has come when the government must decide whether we should allow the same situation to exist in Canada, or whether we should subsidize the farmer in another way. We hear from the government benches that it is not feasible to implement some kind of wage and price controls in Canada. Well, the farmer in Canada has lived with price controls on his commodities for the past 25 years, yet no one has ever controlled his input cost. I think it is high time we decided either to subsidize the farmer or to allow him to charge for his products what they are really worth.
If we are serious about decentralization and moving away from big and cumbersome urban centres, one way of helping the farmer would be to rid him of the burden of property taxes. After all, people who live in cities are helped to surmount the high cost of urban transport and so on. We could devise various ways of helping to improve the quality of rural life by building community facilities, town halls, roads and so forth. A program of this nature would, in my opinion, be more meaningful than anything the minister has laid before us to date.
Another way of helping farmers would be to make available to them, or to community organizations, or regional districts as they arc called in British Columbia, a per capita grant comparable with the grants provincial governments pay in respect of citizens living in municipalities. Farmers and others living in rural areas do
[Mr. Oberle.)
not benefit from such assistance, nor do they benefit as a result of proper representation on municipal or regional governments.
If we could find a way of placing the farmer on an equal basis with Canadians who live in towns and cities we would be doing a great deal to preserve the rural way of life with all its importance to our economy. Property taxes are the means by which institutional facilities such as hospitals and schools are paid for. The time to remove this burden from farmers is long overdue, and the federal government could play a definite role in assisting the provinces to take action along these lines. The Prairie Farm Assistance Act is a good act, but its terms are not broad enough-too few people are eligible to participate and, besides, it is not sufficiently regional in character.
Parts of the rural area I represent are in an early stage of development. None of the programs under the minister's jurisdiction are available to those who are just starting out to be farmers-those who derive a major portion of their income from some other source. They are all dreamers. For the time being they are working as lumbermen, or on oil rigs, or in sawmills. But eventually they would like to be full time farmers. An official of the Farm Credit Corporation will, nevertheless, tell such a person that he is not eligible because he is not a farmer. Nor will he ever be, unless we recognize that there is a need for a change in the legislation.
Were it not for the pioneers, the farm community would not be as well developed as it is today. I believe the act should be amended so as to allow such people to share in some of the benefits of these programs. I realise I am digressing at this point, but for the record it must be said that there are many people in Canada desirous of starting a small business, or upgrading their farming activities, who do not have access to these programs because they are not committed on a full time basis.

Strangely enough, Mr. Chairman, there are farming communities in Newfoundland. On second reading I spoke of the benefits of the wonderful loan plans available to farmers, fishermen and those wishing to enter business, or expand their existing businesses. However, I am wondering whether the Minister of Finance can explain why we, in the Province of Newfoundland, cannot get the benefit of such programs and there are many such programs, about 18, I believe, directed to the small businessman, whether he be a farmer, a fisherman, a hotel operator or a storekeeper.
I can only draw attention again to the reports which have been issued in connection with these loan programs. In the period between January and December, 1972, of loans made in the ten provinces amounting in all to $181 million, four only were made in Newfoundland to a value of $6,546. From January to December, 1973, only three loans were made in the Province of Newfoundland to a value of $8,788 out of a total of over $230 million. And I would remind hon. members that there are areas in my province which have great potential for agricultural production, land which can produce almost all the food requirements of the isolated province of Newfoundland.
I have suggested, Mr. Chairman, that the minister carry out an investigation to determine why bank managers,
April 11, 1974

who are responsible to the Canadian public for carrying out this program, are performing that task in such a way as to produce figures of the kind I have drawn to your attention, with far fewer of these loans going to the province of Newfoundland than to any of the other provinces of Canada.
Hon. members may care to look at the latest report of the activities carried out under the Small Businesses Loans Act. In the period from October to December, 1973, only two loans were granted in Newfoundland amounting to $50,000. From January, 1973, to December of the same year, six loans were granted in the amount of $77,000. And back in 1972, five loans were made to the amount of $58,000. Something has to be wrong, Mr. Chairman. I am sure the minister has received representations from other members of the House, beside myself, pointing out that these loans are not being directed to Newfoundlanders in anything like the proportion allocated to other Canadians. I need hardly add I have no wish to deny to other Canadians the advantages they may derive from this, or similar legislation.
The fishing industry is the mainstay of the Newfoundland economy. But even when it comes to loans under the Fisheries Improvement Loans Act we in Newfoundland are at the bottom of the scale when compared with other coastal provinces. In the period from October to December, 1973, only 14 loans were granted in an amount of $35,000, a sum which does not even reach the maximum figure which the amendment to the act seeks to establish. Even the province of Prince Edward Island, in which the agricultural industry is of major importance, secured 40 loans in an amount of nearly $90,000. In that province, in the period from October to December, 1973, there were 40 loans amounting to $89,000, and in 1972 there were 32 loans amounting to $59,000.
I am hoping that the Minister of Finance, even though he does not listen to the appeal we are making, will realize that something is wrong. I suggest again that this is the fault of the agents who are making these loans, and they are in effect the managers of the branches of the chartered banks. They could not care less for Newfoundlanders. Somebody has to give them a slam over the head, or a kick in the behind, to remind them of their responsibility to Canadians. I hope the minister will take my words of advice and direct that this action, so necessary to the people of Canada, is taken.

Mr. Chairman, I should like to make one or two very brief comments in connection with the amendments to the bill as they relate to the Farm Improvement Loans Act. The increase in the ceiling on loans from $25,000 to $50,000 will be particularly welcomed in the west, as well as the fact that there is no restriction in respect to the use of the money as between land and machinery. I know of many instances when farmers would have welcomed the opportunity to borrow up to $50,000 for the purchase of land, but because they have been tied up with the Farm Credit Corporation they were not able to negotiate a further loan from that source. This will be of considerable help.
One thing that has been brought to my attention from time to time, and this was referred to by the hon. member for Mackenzie and others, is the fact that bank managers seem to discourage the borrowing of money under the Farm Improvement Loans Act. It has been brought to my attention on a number of occasions that when a farmer goes into a bank to borrow money, by the time the manager is through talking to him there are so many obstacles in his way that he borrows the money on the bank's regular plan rather than taking advantage of the lower interest rate available under this act.
As the minister has suggested, it is important that we as members advertise this program, bringing it to the attention of the people concerned. As was suggested by the hon. member for Mackenzie, we should bring the provisions of these acts to the attention of the farmers. Goodness knows, the minister travels from coast to coast and makes I don't know how many speeches a week. As a matter of fact, notes on speeches sent out by the minister's office cross my desk with as much regularity as the daily newspaper from my own constituency.
I would suggest to the minister, when he is speaking around the country, that he point out to the farmers that they can utilize the provisions of these acts. Mr. Chairman, at the outset I should like to congratulate the minister for proposing amendments to this act. One thing that appeals to me is that for the first time this will allow businessmen to enter the money market with the expectation of a certain amount of government assistance. One thing loans under this act are to be used for is the acquisition of land necessary to carry on. At first blush it looks as though this measure might enable the Toronto Northmen, for example, to acquire a football playing field and thus frustrate the desires of the minister's colleague in the Department of National Health and Welfare.
There are a couple of anomalies that have struck me. Several days ago Bill C-20 was introduced to set up the Federal Business Development Bank under the aegis of the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce. According to Clause 4(1) of that bill the objects are as follows:
The objects of the Corporation are to promote and assist in the establishment and development of business enterprises in Canada by providing, in the manner and to the extent authorized by this Act, financial assistance, management counselling, management training, information and advice and such other services as are ancillary or incidental to any of the foregoing.
Then Subclause (2) states:
The Corporation in carrying out its objects shall give particular consideration to the needs of small business enterprises.
I must say I began to be curious because there is no discernible link between this bank which is set up to give assistance to business-as the bill says to give particular consideration to the needs of small business-and the bill which we are now being asked to consider which changes in some respects the Small Businesses Loans Act. I would be pleased if, at the conclusion of my remarks, the minister would clear up what would appear to be an anomaly in the government's approach to small business.
There are other programs which apply to small business. There is a multiplicity of such programs. I shall list some of them. The Federal Business Development Bank, which I have just spoken about, is to take over at least two existing programs.
One is the counselling assistance for small enterprise, the acronym for which is CASE. Another is the business management training program now under the manpower department. It will be taken over by the Business Development Bank. In addition to those two programs there are a few others which are not perhaps widely known to the community. One is called GAAP, the general adjustment assistant program. It was set up to help companies to take advantage of tariff cuts during the Kennedy round of

negotiations. It has now been expanded to include all companies which wish to improve their competitive international situation, or which are faced in the domestic Canadian market with stiff foreign competition.
Under the government's program to broaden aspects of GAAP it has undertaken in some cases to become a partner in the GAAP assistance projects and to take a considerable amount of risk in the process.
There is another program called the program for export market development. Under that program the Department of Industry, Trade and Commerce will provide up to half the cost of forming a consortium of small businesses to trade in foreign markets, as well as some of the initial operating costs. It hopes to get the money back through a share of future sales.
I have outlined just a few programs which apply to small business. One of my colleagues said earlier there were something like 18 in all. I suggest through you, Mr. Chairman, to the Minister of Finance and to his colleagues that despite the fact that he was kind enough to send to my colleague, the hon. member for Hamilton-Wentworth, an attractive and concisely articulated pamphlet, this is a pamphlet which never sees the light of the day in any branches of the chartered banks which I have visited, and that the small businessman .in this country is confused by the multiplicity of programs administered by a variety of departments, ministers, deputy ministers and departmental assistants. What is really needed is a rationalized approach by the establishment of a department of small business under a minister who would administer all the variety of programs which are directed toward the assistance of small business.
When I say "small business" I am talking about medium or smaller enterprises, and it must be remembered that three-fifths of the people of this country, 60 per cent of the working force, work for medium and small business. In the aggregate this is a large sector of the economy. I think the time has long passed when the people who trade in the market and pass as small business should have their relations with the government recognized through the establishment of a separate department. Lord knows how many different departments and ministers they have had to deal with for a long time. I think they deserve a special minister, ministry or department. Our party has pledged that it will set up such a department when we form the government.
I hope, Mr. Chairman, that the exuberant members across the way, who dined well earlier this evening, are having a chance to get it all out.
Mr. Chairman, the breakdown of loans granted in the various provinces during the period January, 1973, to December, 1973, shows that there is no coherent approach to the manner in which the federal government gives assistance to small business. For example, in the provinces of Nova Scotia, Prince Edward Island and Newfoundland there were during that period 163 loans for a total of $1,605,000. That is for three provinces. That compares with $12,587,290 in the province of Quebec, $6,324,986 in the province of Ontario, and $5,268,859 in the province of British Columbia, the three richest provinces in this country. I suggest that there is no per capita justification for this discrepancy.
April 11, 1974

I am not suggesting that there are as many small businesses in the Atlantic provinces as in the other three provinces, but I do suggest it appears, as several of my colleagues have pointed out, that perhaps the government has not done as efficient a job as it might in making small businessmen aware of the facilities and services available to them.
It may very well be that the proper approach, as I have suggested, is a department of small business. I urge this as a consideration for the minister. These are all my remarks except that I would like an explanation from the minister concerning the apparent anomaly I mentioned at the beginning, that is, the connection or lack of it between this bill and the business development bank measure which was introduced a couple of days ago.
