subtopic: EXTERNAL AFFAIRS-POSSIBLE OPENING OF MISSION BY SAUDI ARABIA IN OTTAWA AND CANADIAN EMBASSY IN IRAQ
EXTERNAL AFFAIRS-POSSIBLE OPENING OF MISSION BY SAUDI ARABIA IN OTTAWA AND CANADIAN EMBASSY IN IRAQ
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the question which I asked of the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Sharp) on March 12, and his regrettably inadequate and illusive reply, demonstrate all too clearly and painfully the present government's deplorable disregard of the Arab world over many, many years.
At the moment, in what might be called a deathbed repentance, but which I, with my usual charity, will dub an oilfield repentance, there seems to be some slight indication that there is now a tendency in the government to recognize that there is such a part of the international community as the Arab world. Noting that the United Nations General Assembly some time ago added Arabic to the list of official languages at the premier international body, this is a realistic recognition of the fact that some 130 million people in this world speak that language.
But in its dealing with the Arab world, especially the Middle East areas and the oil producing states, the government has shown an appalling coolness and lack of goodwill to people with whom there is no reason for Canadians
Adjournment Debate
to be on any terms other than friendship. At the moment, for instance, the only Arab countries receiving CIDA aid are those which have French as their second language. There is apparently no thought of programs for such countries as Jordan.
In this particular aspect the government has stumbled with more than usual clumsiness. After the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Macdonald) went through a depressing charade of misinformation regarding Canada's status vis-a-vis the Arab oil embargo, there was an obviously hurried and harried decision to seek closer contacts, diplomatic and commercial, with that very important oil producing country, Saudi Arabia. There was even a move to establish contact with the Emirate States on the gulf. I will not reflect upon the decision to have our ambassador in Tehran at this stage.
I happen to know, through many years of contact and appraisal, that Ambassador George is one of our very best diplomats abroad, but a little thought might have decreed that the designation of an ambassador credited to Iran, which is not an Arab state, might not have been the most astute or felicitous move.
But the major blunder, oversight, slight or affront is the government's obvious panicky decision to open a mission in Saudi Arabia before establishing one in Iraq. Of course we should be in Saudi, should have been there long ago, but we need not have affronted the Iraquis in the process. Iraq has had a well staffed mission with two prestigious ambassadors in Ottawa over a period of many months, but the government has refused to open a mission in Bagdad.
With my colleagues, the hon. members for Selkirk (Mr. Rowland) and Cochrane (Mr. Stewart), I spent 10 days in Iraq and saw at first hand the opportunity for close and more meaningful commercial, cultural and social contacts between our two countries. I saw, too, the representatives of other nations "beating us to the punch" in making meaningful arrangements with Iraq.
I think it most unfortunate, highly irregular and totally unwise to denigrate Iraq by placing in a lower category the opening of a Canadian embassy in Bagdad, after that in Jiddah. Our position is doubly embarrassing when, as I am informed, Saudi Arabia has no early intention of opening a mission in Canada or accrediting its Washington ambassador to Ottawa. We are thus out of alignment in an important sense with both countries.
This reveals not only a low priority for the Arab Middle East, a lack of appreciation of the area to Canada, but also a diplomatic blunder which puts the minister in charge of our foreign policy in the same inept and insensitive category of most of his colleagues, leading us from mistaken judgment to worse in the domestic field.

speakeroldname: Mr. Charles Turner (Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Labour):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Labour
subtopic: EXTERNAL AFFAIRS-POSSIBLE OPENING OF MISSION BY SAUDI ARABIA IN OTTAWA AND CANADIAN EMBASSY IN IRAQ
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am grateful to the hon. member for raising the question of Canada's representation abroad and, in particular, our policy in this respect toward the Middle East.
The government has carried out a policy of expanding Canada's activities abroad in as orderly a manner as is consistent with this country's rapidly evolving and grow-

April 11, 1974
Adjournment Debate
ing interests in the international community. Quite naturally this program of continuing expansion requires increased human and financial resources; expenditures must be controlled and the program necessarily must be phased over a period of time.
In general, we have tried to program openings on a three-year forward planning basis, reconciling competing demands of all the departments of government active overseas. This planning process is under constant review, in order to account for rapidly changing situations. While we attempt to keep the system as responsive to changing requirements as possible, it is obvious, given the restraints I have mentioned, that we cannot always satisfy every requirement immediately.
Hard decisions must be taken and unfortunately these sometimes involve sacrifices we would otherwise prefer not to make. For many years Canada had four diplomatic missions in the Middle East; Beirut, Tel Aviv, Cairo and Tehran. These posts responded to our interests at the time which were, with the exception of UNEF, much less important than they are today or can be expected to be in the future. Consistent with the evolution of the region and Canada's interests in it, the government has attempted to organize its relations with the area to take new realities into account. Thus in recent years we have opened missions in Tunisia, Algeria and Morocco, and recently announced the opening of one in Saudi Arabia. In addition we have taken steps to establish formal diplomatic relations with all other countries in the region; this is now virtually complete.
Recent events have dramatically underscored the importance of the countries of the region for the international community, including Canada. The energy crisis has given added impetus to our planned expansion of representation in the area. The government has, I believe, acted quickly in this regard.
Priorities were in some cases reordered, and our decision to open an embassy in Saudi Arabia was announced in December. No one would deny Saudi Arabia's pivotal role in international affairs, particularly in energy matters, and thus the urgent necessity for Canada to be represented in the Saudi Arabian capital. I can confirm that a Canadian representative is now in Jeddah and that the Department of External Affairs is actively pursuing the necessary administrative arrangements to complete the opening of a fully-staffed embassy by this fall. Similarly, we are giving active consideration to the matter of opening an embassy in Baghdad, Iraq in the near future. We attach considerable importance to our relations with that country, as we know the Government of Iraq does with Canada. Iraq has had an embassy in Canada for more than a year.

subtopic: PENSIONS-RAILWAY EMPLOYEES-INQUIRY AS TO APPOINTMENT OF COMMISSIONER TO CONDUCT INQUIRY
PENSIONS-RAILWAY EMPLOYEES-INQUIRY AS TO APPOINTMENT OF COMMISSIONER TO CONDUCT INQUIRY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to speak tonight on the subject of railway pensions, specifically the government's inertia in resolv-
ing the Canadian National Railways' pension problem. In this context I also intend to make mention of Bill C-139, to amend the Pension Benefit Standards Act. This is a private member's bill designed to pave the way for employees of CNR to get the same pension benefits as members of the public service.
Since the back to work bill of last summer which ordered striking railwaymen back to work, the Minister of Labour (Mr. Munro) has repeatedly assured parliament that the government is studying the plight of the railway pensioners and that the situation is, to quote the minister in an April 1 answer to a question of mine, "under consideration". For almost eight months now the situation has been under review. Only recently the Minister of Labour assured this House that he would be making significant moves in the direction of appointing a commission to go into all aspects of railway pensions.
When does the minister plan to fulfil these commitments? The pension problem is one that will not go away. It must be dealt with immediately. The minister's appointment to Dr. John Deutsch to examine and report on certain aspects of the pension plan is not the way to go about finding a solution to the problem. What is needed in this situation is a committee to look into all, not just some, aspects of the Canadian National pension plan.
It seems to me that any committee or commission would arrive at several conclusions, and should make at least a few of the following recommendations.
First, that all participants in the CN pension plan be entitled to equal benefits, and to this end support should be given for extension of the 2 per cent formula, retroactive to the first day of service, as an objective of future collective bargaining.
Second, that CN pension survivor benefits be equivalent to the public service plan.
Third, that the principle of the cost of living index escalation in CN pensions be on the same basis as pensions payable by the federal government generally, and that this escalation be extended to retired railway pensioners in the same way as it has been extended to other federal pensioners.
Fourth, that the widows of all CN pensioners be entitled to survivor benefits, and that immediate action be taken to provide survivor benefits to widows of members of the 1935 plan.
Fifth, that a full evaluation at regular intervals of the benefits, structure and financing of the CN pension fund be made by an independent commissioner. Such evaluation should pertain as well to the situation facing retired railway pensioners. It would determine the moneys available for the financing of its benefit recommendations and suggest positive measures, where necessary, to keep the fund on a sound footing.
It is time the minister gave a committee of the House the opportunity to make such recommendations, all of which would drastically improve the situation of the CNR pensioners. Or will the government do anything to improve the situation? One has to wonder in view of Bill C-139, a bill which, in fairness to my friend, the hon. member for St. Boniface (Mr. Guay), is one of noble intention.
April 11, 1974

That bill, which would give the same pension benefits to CNR employees as those received by public service employees has, as is the case with most private members' bills, little chance of passing into law. This is unfortunate because amendments to the Pension Benefits Standards Act would result in a distinct improvement in CNR pensions. The amendment would remove the CNR from the scope of the act. Such a move, without adding substantially to CNR's annual deficit, would improve its pension plan by providing pensions for its existing and retired employees on a basis similar to that applicable to the public service.
So much for the content of the bill, but the interesting thing about it is the manner in which it has been presented, for here we have one off those rare birds, a government backbencher, introducing a private member's bill with the apparent backing of his entire party. To me this is rather peculiar. After all when a government wants certain legislation passed in parliament, is it not the usual practice for the appropriate minister to introduce it? Is it not true that the government has a much better chance to pass legislation when it is presented in that manner and not via a private member's bill? Is it not true that private members' bills have a notoriously low record of success?
The conclusion one draws from this sham relating to Bill C-139 is obvious. The government does not really want to improve the lot of CN pensioners and, in an effort to cover up this fact and save face, the hon. member for St. Boniface has been delegated to introduce a private member's bill which, however admirable, has little chance of passing. It is indeed unfortunate that the Minister of Labour (Mr. Munro) has chosen to confront the entire problem of CNR pensions in this manner. What is needed is sincerity and a fulfilment of those commitments which were made to CNR pensioners. If the best the government can do is this private member's bill, then by all means let us pass it, but I think the Minister of Labour can and should do more immediately.

speakeroldname: Mr. Charles Turner (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Labour):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Labour
subtopic: PENSIONS-RAILWAY EMPLOYEES-INQUIRY AS TO APPOINTMENT OF COMMISSIONER TO CONDUCT INQUIRY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as has been explained recently in this House and elsewhere, the matter of railway pensions is one under close review by the government of Canada. It is a complex problem, cutting across departmental responsibilities and, since the last round of labour negotiations in the industry, involving a collective bargaining relationship.
As the Minister of Labour (Mr. Munro) has said in response to questions in the House on previous occasions, he has had under serious consideration the appointment of an inquiry commission with broad terms of reference to examine both the costs and benefit structure of railway pension plans. However, he did state that he was of the view that the parties, that is, the railways and the various bargaining groups of railway unions, should perhaps be afforded an opportunity to look at the matter of pensions themselves prior to making a final determination as to
Adjournment Debate
whether or not he should recommend the appointment of an industrial inquiry commission into the matter.
As you are no doubt aware, Judge Hall, in his arbitration award, reserved final decision on several matters that were in dispute. The most important of these, of course, is the question of job security based on the principle of attrition.
I am sure that members of the House will appreciate that most of the railways and the unions involved are, and will continue to be, very deeply involved in meetings concerning the various studies that have to be made in respect of a job security plan, because they must be in a position to report back to Judge Hall by the end of June, at which time they will have to report to Judge Hall on whether or not they have been able to negotiate an agreement on their own.
From the above one can see that officials of the railways and the unions are heavily involved in continuous meetings with the parties for further discussions on the matter of pensions.
As the minister said on March 11, he has some further information that he is checking into for accuracy, but all of the facts and information have been made available and assessed in depth, and I am sure that the minister will be only too pleased to make a further announcement on this extremely important matter.
The government attaches great importance to the question of pensions in the railway industry. That is precisely why a good deal of thought and consideration is being given to it, not only in the Department of Labour but in other concerned departments such as the Department of Transport and the department of insurance. However, as important as the problem is, it should not be allowed to obscure a number of improvements which have been made recently.
As the Minister of Labour has stated, the railway pension plan following the last bargaining round has now become among the best in Canada. In some aspects it surpasses the pension plan of the Public Service of Canada. Successive plans have helped to do away with many of the anomalies and inequities that are virtually inevitable in any scheme the size of the railways plan. Everyone is aware, of course, of the tremendous efforts made when the House of Commons Standing Committee on Transport and Communications dealt with the question of the CN pension fund in September, 1970. Improvements were made both during and after the time that the committee hearings were held.
Some problems, of course, still exist. The concern of many long service railway workers that the improved 2 per cent formula should have been applied for since prior to 1956, is an example. However, we are confident that, with the help of experienced and responsible railway union leadership, as well as with co-operation from the companies, problem areas can be resolved to the benefit of railway workers.
